questions.material:
Mina had spent a month planning the astronomy club's first evening outdoors. She had chosen a field, borrowed a small telescope and made a list of things to observe. On the afternoon of the event, however, thick clouds (1) ____ across the sky. She wanted to cancel before anyone arrived.

Mr Green, the club adviser, asked what she had promised the visitors. “A chance to look at the night sky,” she said. “Not a (2) ____ that it would be clear,” he replied. He suggested explaining the situation and letting people (3) ____ whether to come. Mina sent a message describing the clouds and the indoor activities they could offer instead. Half the visitors still came.

At first, she kept (4) ____ for the weather. Then a younger student asked how a telescope worked. Mina used two simple drawings to explain the parts. She had expected this explanation to take a minute, but the students' questions (5) ____ it into a lively discussion. Nobody was checking the (6) ____ to see how much time was left.

Later, a visitor noticed a small opening between the clouds. Mina quickly (7) ____ the group outside. They took turns looking through the telescope before the gap closed. The view lasted only a few minutes, but the waiting had made everyone more (8) ____. Even the quietest student asked to look again.

While packing up, Mina found that her observation sheet was nearly (9) ____. She had been too busy answering questions to record much. A visitor offered to share his notes, and several others added details. Together, they (10) ____ a record of the night's brief view.

The evening had not followed Mina's plan, yet it had not been a (11) ____. Her careful preparation had given her something to (12) ____ when the weather changed. What helped most was (13) ____ the visitors in the new plan. She had arrived expecting to be the person with all the answers. She left with a record that (14) ____ to the whole group and a better idea of what it meant to (15) ____ an event.

Our class was collecting items for a charity sale. I brought an ordinary teapot, unused in our cupboard for years. I thought it would be (1) ____ to sell. Before I packed it, Grandfather asked whether I knew its history.

I assumed Grandfather had bought it. Grandfather explained that his first neighbour had given it to him when both families were new to the town. The teapot had once been used at their weekly (2) ____. Hearing this, I began to see it as more than an unwanted (3) ____.

At school, my friend Leo read my description and asked a question I had (4) ____: had Grandfather agreed to the sale? I had told him about the sale, but I had never asked him (5) ____ about this particular item.

That evening, Grandfather agreed to the sale but asked me to (6) ____ one detail in my description. The neighbour had not made the teapot himself; he had chosen it as a gift. I had added the story about making it because it sounded more (7) ____. I crossed that sentence out.

On the day of the sale, a visitor spent several minutes reading the card. She did not offer a large amount, but she said she would use the teapot when her own neighbours came round. Her plan (8) ____ me. I had been thinking mainly about the money it might (9) ____.

Afterwards, I told Grandfather about the buyer. He looked (10) ____, not sad. “A cupboard is a quiet place for something made to be shared,” he said.

The class collected enough money for its project. My teapot was not the most expensive item, but its journey had taught me to ask for (11) ____, keep a story (12) ____ and notice a buyer's intention. I had started by trying to clear a shelf. I finished by understanding why a simple object might carry (13) ____ that a price could not measure. The sale gave it a new home without (14) ____ its past. I kept a photograph of the teapot and the (15) ____ description, ready to show Grandfather when I next visited.

I offered to take photographs for our neighbourhood animal shelter. I imagined friendly dogs facing the camera. But Pip, the first dog, had other (1) ____. Whenever I lifted the camera, he turned away and hid beside a chair.

I tried calling his name more loudly, but he moved even (2) ____ away. A volunteer who had cared for Pip for weeks asked me to lower my voice and sit. He needed time with (3) ____, she explained. I put the camera beside me and waited.

Ten minutes passed. I thought I was wasting the afternoon. Then Pip came out to examine a soft toy near my shoe. I reached for the camera, and he (4) ____. This time I understood: my sudden movement had interrupted a small moment of (5) ____.

The volunteer suggested watching before trying again. I noticed that Pip returned to the toy whenever the room was (6) ____. So I sat still, with the camera ready in my lap. When he eventually settled down, I took one photograph without standing up.

The picture was not what I had (7) ____. Pip was looking at the toy, not at me. Yet his ears were relaxed, and the volunteer said the photograph showed a side of him that visitors rarely (8) ____. We decided to use it with a short description explaining that he was shy at first.

A week later, a woman came to meet Pip after seeing the picture. She did not (9) ____ him to rush towards her. She sat by the chair and waited for him to approach. The volunteer arranged further visits before any decision was made.

I had wanted a photograph that would make Pip look instantly (10) ____. What he needed was one that represented him (11) ____. The camera could record a moment; it could not create the trust I had tried to (12) ____. After that afternoon, I changed my approach. I asked volunteers about each animal and allowed more time for the (13) ____.

Some days I came home with only a few usable pictures. I no longer counted that as poor (14) ____. A successful photograph was not simply one that looked impressive. It was one made with enough (15) ____ for the subject's needs.

questions.material:
Our monthly readers’ column brings together four invented books chosen by the Harbour Reading Circle. Each recommendation comes from a different reader. These are introductions, not extracts, and no knowledge of other books is needed. Which would you put on your next reading list?

A1

The Last Platform — a novel by Mira Venn
When a railway line is about to close, sixteen-year-old Jo finds a box of unsigned postcards in its waiting room. Each chapter follows a different card to a former passenger, whose memory changes Jo’s first impression of the station. The mystery is not about a crime: it concerns who has kept the old room open, and why. Reader Evan likes the way ordinary journeys become a shared history.

A2

Between Two Covers — a memoir by Ada Pell
Pell recalls her first year repairing damaged books in a small workshop. She describes failed attempts as carefully as successful repairs and explains why an almost invisible stain can matter to an owner. There are no step-by-step repair instructions. Reader Suri recommends it to people interested in learning a craft through patient observation rather than buying tools immediately.

A3

Borrowed Light — a collection by Niko Vale
These short poems follow the changing view from one apartment window over a year. A travelling reflection, a neighbour’s curtain and a streetlamp become starting points for thoughts about distance. Reader Tom enjoys reading just one poem before breakfast. He warns anyone looking for a continuous plot that the collection deliberately leaves spaces between its separate scenes.

A4

The Quiet Orbit — a science-fiction novel by Lin Daro
A repair crew aboard an imaginary space station receives messages that seem to arrive before they are sent. The characters test several explanations instead of accepting the most exciting one. Reader Mei particularly enjoys the tense discussions: solving the puzzle depends on colleagues comparing incomplete records, not on a lone hero winning a fight. The story’s machines and physical rules are inventions.

questions.material:
B1

At the opening of the fictional Riverfold Design Exchange, visitors expecting a display of old festival lamps instead walked between tall screens of moving light. The screens carried patterns drawn from paper lanterns once made in the district. Twelve young designers had worked with six retired makers, but the final objects were intended for contemporary indoor spaces, not for use in a traditional ceremony.

The project began with a disagreement. Some designers wanted to photograph the lamps and copy their outlines onto fabric. Maker Wen objected that this would preserve the surface while losing the way a lantern was built. She opened an unfinished frame and showed how each narrow strip supported the next. The teams then used that principle of linked supports to develop folding screens. Visitors could see both the old frame and the new joints beside it.

The exchange was organised to let local makers and visiting design students learn from one another. Sales were not its measure of success: the objects were not offered for purchase. Instead, each team kept a record of a decision it had changed after talking to its partners. One student replaced a rigid plastic edge after Wen demonstrated how a flexible strip survived repeated folding.

Early public reactions were tentative. Several visitors said they needed to walk around the screens before deciding what they thought. By the end of the evening, the discussion board contained questions about construction as well as comments on appearance. Curator Sela called that a useful change. “A pattern may catch your eye,” she said, “but asking how it works can start a longer conversation.” The organisers plan another exchange, while admitting that one evening cannot show whether those conversations will continue.

C. Its camera plate connects to a phone.

questions.material:
C1

Trying to keep a camera level on a narrow bird-watching platform can turn an enjoyable morning into a struggle. The fictional FieldRest stand is designed for that awkward space between a pocket tripod and a large professional support. This product introduction describes the maker’s proposed model; its features are part of an invented advertising scenario, not independently tested performance claims.

FieldRest folds into a flat rectangle that slides into the side pocket of its supplied case. Three legs open from the centre, but they do not have to be extended to equal lengths. On an uneven surface, you can adjust each one separately while watching a small level window. The camera plate stays attached to your camera, so attaching the camera to the stand requires one locking movement rather than repeatedly turning a screw. A red mark remains visible until the lock is fully closed.

If complicated controls have put you off similar equipment, notice the two large adjustment wheels. Each can be turned with gloves on. No phone account, wireless connection or software update is required. The maker includes a printed practice card so that you can rehearse opening and locking the stand at home before taking it outdoors. This example is meant to show ease of handling, not to promise that every user will obtain sharp photographs.

The standard pack costs 84 fictional credits and includes the stand, camera plate, case and practice card. A replacement plate costs extra. The stated maximum supported camera weight is two kilograms, and the instructions exclude use in moving vehicles or strong wind. A strap holds the folded legs together during transport; it is not a safety line for suspending a camera.

For a photographer who values a compact support without electronic controls, FieldRest offers an appealing option. Check your camera’s weight and the stated conditions before ordering. The maker’s return offer covers an unused stand returned within fourteen days, so practise the movements without mounting a camera if you may wish to return it.

options.text: A. The corridor the participants had to walk through.
B. The style of the route symbols.
C. The number of turns on the route.
D. The maximum time allowed for studying.

questions.material:
D1

Would a map be easier to remember if its symbols resembled the places they represented? An invented study at Bellwater College explored that question with a simple indoor route. Its results suggest a possible design choice, but the researchers stress that remembering a short route in a quiet building is different from finding a safe path through a crowded town.

The team recruited forty adult volunteers who had never visited the test corridor. Participants were assigned by a random draw to two equal groups. Both received a map showing the same six turns and room positions. One version used small drawings of objects, such as a cup for a refreshment room; the other used plain numbered circles. Everyone studied the map for two minutes, then returned it and walked the route. A researcher recorded wrong turns without offering directions.

The drawing group made fewer wrong turns on average. It also took longer to study the map within the permitted two minutes. Because the team had changed the symbol style while keeping the route, room positions and study-time limit the same, the comparison provides some evidence about that design change in these conditions. It does not show that drawings make people remember every kind of information better. Nor does it establish what would happen if map users could consult the map while walking.

A second observation helped explain what the volunteers did. After the walk, several drawing-group participants described a sequence of pictured objects, while several number-group participants recalled a string of digits. The team suggests that meaningful pictures may give a route a memorable sequence. These comments are clues to a possible explanation, not a direct measurement of the mental process itself.

Independent reviewer Dr Sol welcomed the careful comparison but urged restraint. The sample was small, all participants were adults, and they were tested immediately. Children, longer delays and busy outdoor routes were not studied. Before changing public wayfinding systems, Sol recommended larger trials with different users and checks on readability at a distance. The team agreed and described its next task as testing the limits of the effect, rather than selling a universal map design.

options.text: A. A Door in the Rain.
B. One River, Many Names.
C. Under the Stage.
D. The Longest Afternoon.

questions.material:
Four members of the North Quay Book Club introduce imaginary books they have recently enjoyed. Their choices range from a graphic novel to a journey in diary form. Send the club a recommendation of your own for next month’s readers’ page; describe what makes your choice distinctive.

A1

A Door in the Rain — a graphic novel by Etta Noll
A delivery rider keeps finding the same painted door in different streets. The illustrations give clues that the characters’ speech sometimes misses. Reader Amir recommends looking closely at the edges of each frame before turning the page. Although the setting seems mysterious, the final explanation grows from the neighbours’ shared effort to protect a local artwork, rather than from magic.

A2

One River, Many Names — a travel diary by Sami Orr
Orr follows a small river from its source to the sea, recording a new entry each evening. Meetings with ferrymen, walkers and people living beside the water change the questions Orr asks. Reader June values the admission that a traveller sees only part of a place. Maps indicate the journey, but this is a personal account, not a guide to safe river travel.

A3

Under the Stage — a memoir by Faye Dem
Before becoming a set builder, Dem worked out of sight in a travelling theatre. She remembers hurried changes, wrong measurements and a patient supervisor who asked her to explain every design choice. Reader Noor says the account made backstage work feel important without making it look easy. Readers wanting a famous actor’s life story should choose something else.

A4

The Longest Afternoon — a verse novel by Cal Rinn
Short poems tell a continuous story about two cousins waiting for a relative’s delayed arrival. A familiar room gradually becomes strange as they invent competing explanations for the delay. Reader Leo likes how the cousins revise those explanations when messages arrive. Unlike a collection of unrelated poems, the book follows one afternoon from the first missed bus to the final knock at the door.

questions.material:
Four members of the North Quay Book Club introduce imaginary books they have recently enjoyed. Their choices range from a graphic novel to a journey in diary form. Send the club a recommendation of your own for next month’s readers’ page; describe what makes your choice distinctive.

A1

A Door in the Rain — a graphic novel by Etta Noll
A delivery rider keeps finding the same painted door in different streets. The illustrations give clues that the characters’ speech sometimes misses. Reader Amir recommends looking closely at the edges of each frame before turning the page. Although the setting seems mysterious, the final explanation grows from the neighbours’ shared effort to protect a local artwork, rather than from magic.

A2

One River, Many Names — a travel diary by Sami Orr
Orr follows a small river from its source to the sea, recording a new entry each evening. Meetings with ferrymen, walkers and people living beside the water change the questions Orr asks. Reader June values the admission that a traveller sees only part of a place. Maps indicate the journey, but this is a personal account, not a guide to safe river travel.

A3

Under the Stage — a memoir by Faye Dem
Before becoming a set builder, Dem worked out of sight in a travelling theatre. She remembers hurried changes, wrong measurements and a patient supervisor who asked her to explain every design choice. Reader Noor says the account made backstage work feel important without making it look easy. Readers wanting a famous actor’s life story should choose something else.

A4

The Longest Afternoon — a verse novel by Cal Rinn
Short poems tell a continuous story about two cousins waiting for a relative’s delayed arrival. A familiar room gradually becomes strange as they invent competing explanations for the delay. Reader Leo likes how the cousins revise those explanations when messages arrive. Unlike a collection of unrelated poems, the book follows one afternoon from the first missed bus to the final knock at the door.

questions.material:
B1

At the fictional Alder House Arts Centre, a new exhibition pairs traditional shadow puppets with moving sculptures made by design students. Visitors can look behind each screen to see the rods and joints. The organisers want the exhibition to reveal a working relationship between older performers and young makers, rather than present tradition as a collection of silent shapes.

The partnership began when puppeteer Mara watched a student’s model bird. Its painted wings resembled those on a puppet from her company, but they moved independently, producing a jerky flight. Mara demonstrated how a single rod could make two wings rise together. The student retained the pattern but rebuilt the movement around that connection. Alongside the finished sculpture stands the awkward first model, so that visitors can compare what changed.

Other teams went in different directions. One turned a sliding stage doorway into a panel that reveals several scenes as it moves. Another used the shape of a puppet’s hand to make a handle easier to grip. None of the teams claims that these objects can replace a live shadow performance. They are experiments in carrying a practical idea into a new setting.

The exhibition’s publicity is deliberately restrained. Instead of promising a revolution in design, the leaflet invites visitors to notice one small change and discuss it. Each label names both partners and records an idea that each contributed. “If only the finished object gets attention, people may think the student worked alone,” says curator Ivo. “We want the conversation to remain visible.”

During the opening weekend, visitors left sketches of movements they wanted to understand. The centre will use these requests to choose demonstrations for a later workshop. It has not yet measured whether visitors remember the ideas, but the requests give the organisers something more specific than a simple count of people through the door.

questions.material:
C1

An oversized drawing folder can be surprisingly difficult to carry across a campus. The fictional PaperPort cart offers art students a way to move large, flat work while leaving their hands free to open a door. The description here belongs to an invented product campaign; it is not a report of independent trials or a claim about a real manufacturer.

PaperPort has a wide vertical frame fitted with two soft straps. Slip a closed portfolio into the frame, tighten the straps, and pull the cart by its height-adjustable handle. The wheels sit outside the frame so that a broad folder does not rub against them. The lower support folds upward when the cart is empty, allowing it to hang on a wall hook. A removable cover is included for light rain, though the maker specifically excludes heavy rain and immersion from its protection claim.

The handle has three marked height settings. Pressing a large side button releases it; there is no small screw to loosen. In the campaign’s example, a student wearing paint-stained gloves changes the setting without removing them. The example highlights an accessible control, not a medical claim that the cart is suitable for every person with limited hand movement. Users should check whether they can operate the button comfortably.

The basic pack costs  sixty fictional credits and carries a stated maximum load of eight kilograms. It includes the cover and a sheet showing how to secure different portfolio sizes. It does not include a portfolio. Replacement straps can be ordered separately, and the wheels can be removed with the supplied tool if a worn wheel needs changing. There is no motor or battery to charge.

Would PaperPort fit your routine? Measure your folder before ordering: the supported width range is printed beside the purchase button. The cart is intended for reasonably smooth paths and cannot make steps disappear. If you often carry drawings between ground-floor studios, however, its folding support and simple controls may remove one awkward part of the journey. The campaign invites prospective buyers to try an unloaded model at the campus shop before choosing.

questions.material:
D1

A ringing reminder can attract attention, but can a silent visual change do the same job without interrupting a workshop? A fictional team at Redmere Institute tested a thin border that slowly changed colour around an on-screen drawing task. The study considered whether adults noticed a break reminder, not whether taking breaks improves health or the quality of their artwork.

Forty-eight volunteers attended the same introductory digital drawing session. By random assignment, half saw a small written break reminder appear after twelve minutes. The other half saw the same words in the same place, surrounded by a border that gradually changed from grey to blue. Both messages remained on screen for thirty seconds. questions.material:
Welcome to the invented Pebble Street readers’ page. This month’s four recommendations concern places that change as people look at them differently. The books and their authors are fictional. Read these short descriptions to choose a story or account that matches your interests.

A1

The Room Above the Shop — a novel by Sel Arven
A teenager clearing an unused room finds labels for objects that are no longer there. She interviews former shop workers to reconstruct the room’s changing purpose. Some memories disagree, and she must preserve the disagreement instead of forcing a neat answer. Reader Lani admires a mystery in which learning to ask better questions matters more than finding a hidden treasure.

A2

Lines Along the Shore — illustrated essays by Bo Renn
Renn sketches temporary marks left by ropes, waves and wheels beside an imaginary harbour. Each drawing is accompanied by a short reflection on what can and cannot be inferred from a trace. Reader Deniz recommends it for short reading sessions. The essays can be read in any order, and the book does not offer a continuous adventure plot.

A3

A Seat for Everyone — a memoir by Ina Kest
Kest looks back on helping to run a tiny community cinema. Problems with seating, borrowed curtains and stubborn disagreements occupy more space than glamorous film premieres. Reader Hal enjoys the honest accounts of mistakes and the gradual discovery that welcoming an audience requires listening. It is a personal recollection, not a technical handbook for building a cinema.

A4

After the Signal — a science-fiction novel by Teo Marr
A distant settlement receives a message consisting only of a pause repeated at different intervals. An engineer and a musician propose rival explanations, then design tests they can both accept. Reader Wen likes their changing partnership and the way a confident guess becomes a question again. The settlement, signal and technologies exist only in the story; they are not a report of a real discovery.

questions.material:
B1

Fragments that once lay in boxes beneath a workshop have become the starting point for a fictional exhibition at Moorwell Gallery. Ceramic workers and young furniture designers jointly created a set of small stools inspired by broken decorative tiles. The display does not present damaged tiles as rubbish to be hidden. It asks how a fragment can suggest a new way to arrange colour and space.

At first, the designers planned to copy complete patterns from photographs of tiled walls. Ceramic worker Dara proposed a different beginning. She gave each team three irregular fragments and asked them to trace the edges, including the broken ones. One team found that the gaps between its traced shapes formed a pattern as interesting as the coloured pieces themselves. It developed a stool seat with an open centre rather than a surface covered by copied flowers.

The collaboration was organised to share methods across crafts. Each team had to explain one choice to a partner who used different materials. A furniture student learned that a thin-looking tile edge was stronger when supported in a particular direction. Dara in turn changed the display label after a student asked her to explain a specialist word. Neither partner was treated simply as a supplier of attractive shapes.

The first seating plan for the gallery was provisional. After visitors in a trial session struggled to move between the stools, the organisers left more space and added a route around the outside. The objects could still be viewed closely, but visitors were no longer forced into a narrow central path.

Gallery director Ula says that the changes in the plan reflect the exchange itself. “We did not begin with a finished solution and then invite people to admire it,” she explains. “We let other people’s experience change what we made.” The gallery has recorded the process beside each object. Whether it will lead to lasting partnerships remains an open question for the next year.

questions.material:
C1

Books do not always stay open where you want them, especially when you are following a diagram and need both hands. The fictional PageAngle reading stand is designed to hold a book at a chosen slope on a desk. This is an invented promotional description: the performance and price belong to the scenario and should not be taken as independent findings about a real product.

PageAngle uses a broad base with a supporting panel that clicks into four positions. Two sliding clips rest gently on the lower corners of the open pages. Their clear tips leave the page numbers visible, and each clip can be moved separately when you turn a page. The maker recommends testing the clips on a few pages first; valuable or fragile books are excluded from the intended uses. The clips cannot make a damaged binding safe.

A low front lip keeps a thick book from sliding onto the desk. When you are finished, the panel folds against the base and the clips fit into shallow slots. The folded stand is small enough for the maker’s supplied cloth sleeve. A short printed card illustrates the four positions and the release catch. In the campaign’s demonstration, a new user changes the angle without a tool. The example emphasises ease of adjustment, rather than claiming that a particular angle will cure discomfort.

The standard pack is priced at  thirty-six fictional credits, including the sleeve and instruction card. The stated book-weight limit is three kilograms. Replacement clips are available at an additional charge, but there is no electric light, automatic page turner or charging socket hidden in the base. Buyers looking for those functions should choose a different product.

If you regularly move between reading and practical work at the same desk, a fold-flat support may suit you better than a fixed shelf. Check the open book’s width against the dimensions before buying. The seller offers a display model for testing at its shop and advises customers to bring a similarly sized ordinary book. That small check can help you decide whether PageAngle fits your work, rather than relying only on the photographs.

questions.material:
D1

When people revise a notice, does a short checklist help them find problems that a general instruction misses? In a fictional experiment at Haven Learning Lab, adult volunteers revised a notice for a community room. The team measured corrections to that particular text. It did not attempt to measure a permanent improvement in writing ability.

Sixty volunteers were assigned at random to two groups. Everyone received the same notice containing a wrong opening time, an unclear booking address and a missing statement about bringing identification. They also received a separate information sheet giving the correct details. One group was simply asked to make the notice useful to a new visitor. The other received that instruction plus a three-item checklist asking them to verify time, booking location and required documents. Both groups had five minutes and could consult the information sheet throughout.

The checklist group corrected more of the three target problems on average. However, the team had provided both the checklist structure and specific prompts about what to check. The experiment cannot show whether a blank checklist, with its headings removed, would be equally useful. It supports a claim about this guided revision activity, not a claim that every list improves every piece of writing.

The researchers also counted unnecessary changes to correct information. The checklist group did not clearly differ from the other group on that measure. Keeping this result separate mattered: fixing a target error and avoiding a new error are different achievements. A single total labelled “better writing” would have concealed that distinction.

Reviewer Dr Elin welcomed the practical comparison but cautioned against using the findings to advertise a general writing course. The volunteers were adults, the task was short, and they had the correct information beside them. The study did not test whether they could identify problems in a new text without prompts a week later. Elin proposed a follow-up with unfamiliar notices and delayed tests. The team agreed that such evidence was needed before making claims about independent revision skills.

options.text: A. To choose a new room for the lunchtime club.
B. To learn whether shade would make the seating area more useful.
C. To find the cheapest cloth sold near the school.
D. To compare students' opinions of different teachers.

questions.material:
At Northbank School, where courtyard seats were exposed to direct sunlight, students often avoided them at lunchtime, leading the student council to suggest a light roof above one seating area. Before asking the school to pay for it, a small team wanted to find out whether shade would make the area more useful.

For one week, the team placed a temporary cloth cover above six seats, counting how many were occupied at twelve thirty each day and asking users whether they would return. The numbers looked encouraging because more students sat there than in the previous week, while several users also said they preferred the covered seats.

However, science teacher Ms Ray asked what else had changed between the two weeks that might help explain the increase. A popular lunchtime club had moved to a room beside the courtyard, where students waiting for it often used the seats, and the weather had also been cooler. Either change might have affected the count, which showed that the covered area was being used without establishing how much of the increase had been caused by shade.

For their next test, the team used two areas with the same number of seats, one of which had a cover while the other did not, recording both at the same time over several days. They noted weather and nearby activities and asked students why they chose an area, recognising that this comparison, though unable to remove every possible difference, would provide a clearer picture than comparing different weeks.

The council then revised its report, retaining the positive comments while adding the limits of the first test and explaining what further evidence was needed. "We still think a roof is worth considering," said council member Ella. "But a recommendation is stronger when readers can see what it is based on, including what we haven't established yet."

questions.material:
Working Together in a School Club

A school club does not need a large room or expensive equipment to be useful. What it needs is a way for members to work together regularly. [1] The following ideas can help a new club make a good start.

Keep the plan visible.

When a group agrees to make a short film, write down who will bring the camera and who will prepare the story. [2] A member who misses a meeting can then check the page rather than ask everyone to repeat the decision.

Share more than the finished work.

At a meeting, someone may show a poster and simply say, "I made this." Other members may admire the colours but learn little about the process. [3] Questions like these let people understand choices, and they can offer more useful suggestions.

Make mistakes easy to report.

A member who deletes a sound recording by accident may be tempted to hide it. The club leader has a choice about how to reply. [4] That response tells the member that honesty is welcome, even when the news is inconvenient. It makes it more likely that the group will hear about the problem while there is still time to record again.

[5]

Some problems need help from outside the group. A science teacher may show members how to use a sensor safely, while a member of the school media team may explain how to borrow a microphone. Explain what you are trying to do and ask a specific question. Asking for help is different from expecting someone else to finish the project for you.

A. Thank the member for explaining the problem before discussing a solution.
B. Put this list on a page that every member can read.
C. Colourful posters can attract attention before a club holds its first meeting.
D. A few clear routines can make that cooperation easier.
E. Invite more students.
F. Ask for specific help.
G. Ask what the maker changed and which idea did not work.

questions.material:
The following account describes a fictional drama workshop. Its director, Mara, noticed that actors could repeat her instructions accurately and still seem uncertain about the next rehearsal. They remembered comments such as “leave more space” but no longer recalled which moment of the scene each comment concerned. Her notes had preserved the words while losing their connection to an action.

Mara asked an assistant, Felix, to divide a recording into short scenes. Actors could attach a written note to a particular moment and explain what they hoped to try next. Felix's job was to make those moments easy to locate; he was not asked to decide whether an interpretation was dramatically convincing. That judgement remained with the people rehearsing together.

The workshop described the new record as “a set of handles, not a finished performance”. The handles helped actors pick up an interrupted line of work. A marked moment could remind them where an idea had arisen, but it could not make the artistic choice for them. Two actors might attach different notes to the same pause, and that difference could start a useful conversation rather than indicate an error in the system.

During a trial, fewer rehearsal minutes were spent searching for the scene under discussion. The director did not conclude that every performance had therefore improved. Some actors wrote too much and found their own notes hard to use. Mara consequently kept the system optional and introduced a short review at the end of each session, when actors could remove notes that no longer helped. The record was valuable when it supported their attention, not when maintaining it became a second performance demanding attention of its own.

questions.material:
This fictional account concerns a small public garden preparing signs in two languages. Its volunteers initially fed short plant descriptions into a translation tool and printed the results. The difficulty was not simply that a few words were wrong. Some descriptions used “here” and “this corner” even though the printer had combined sentences from different locations. A fluent sentence could therefore point a visitor towards the wrong bed.

The garden manager, Rosa, changed the process. A volunteer first photographed the intended location and wrote a short explanation of what a visitor should learn there. A translator then used that explanation and the draft text together. The software could suggest wording, but responsibility for checking the reference remained with the person reviewing the sign at its actual site. The printer received only the approved version.

Rosa called the photograph “an anchor for the words”. She did not mean that every object in the image had to be described. The image kept a phrase such as “on your right” attached to a particular viewpoint. Without that link, a sentence could be correct in grammar and still give incorrect guidance. Nor did the photograph supply the translation itself; it helped a reviewer ask whether the translation referred to the right thing.

The new procedure took longer before printing. It also caught several mismatches that a check of spelling alone had missed. Rosa did not treat those examples as proof that the tool was useless. The volunteers still used its suggestions, especially when comparing short alternatives. They had simply stopped treating a smooth first draft as a finished sign. Later feedback from visitors would be needed to find out whether the approved signs were easy to use as well as correctly located.

questions.material:
A campus sound walk can help a group notice places it usually crosses without much attention. Participants record short sounds and link them to stops on a route. The project needs clear choices about recording, listening and publication.

Decide what a stop should reveal

A recording is more useful when it has a purpose. At a busy doorway, for example, the group might want listeners to notice the rhythm of arrivals rather than identify particular speakers. (1) ____ A clear aim can keep the group from collecting long recordings simply because the device has enough space.

Keep a location record

A file name such as “new sound 7” gives little help a week later. (2) ____ The notes need not describe every noise, but they should allow another member to find the intended place. Otherwise, a sound may be placed beside the wrong stop on the route.

Check what may be shared

A sound made in a public part of a school is not automatically something the group should publish. Follow the school's recording rules and obtain any required permission. (3) ____ Leaving a recording unpublished is a reasonable choice when those conditions have not been met.

Before the final route is announced, ask someone outside the group to follow it. (4) ____ Where a listener cannot locate a stop or understand an instruction, change the route notes. This is a test of the instructions, not a competition to identify the most sounds.

(5) ____

Keep a copy of the approved files together with their location notes and permission record. If the route changes, review those links before reusing the recordings. A useful archive preserves the conditions under which its material can be understood and shared.

questions.material:
For our school radio play, I wanted the leading role. Instead, I was asked to produce the sound effects. I took the decision as a (1) ____: someone else would receive the applause while I stayed behind a curtain. At the first rehearsal, I barely listened to the actors. When rain was mentioned, I shook a tin of dry peas without waiting for the director's (2) ____. The noise drowned out a crucial line.
Afterwards, the youngest actor approached me. I expected a (3) ____, but she asked how I had made the rain. She had imagined real water falling into a bucket. Her curiosity (4) ____ me enough to explain the trick. As we experimented together, I noticed that a gentle movement produced a shower, while a rapid one suggested a storm. The same tin could express different (5) ____.
At the next rehearsal, I followed the script with a pencil. Rather than interrupting every mention of weather, I waited for a (6) ____ in the dialogue. This time, the rain seemed to belong to the scene. The director asked me to make it gradually fade as the character's fear (7) ____.
On performance day, the tin slipped from my hand just before my final cue. I caught it, but the peas had spilled. For a second, I (8) ____. Then I remembered the sheet of thin paper beside me. I rubbed it softly and (9) ____ the missing sound. Nobody in the audience saw the change.
At the end, the actors invited the crew forward. I was pleased, but the public (10) ____ was no longer the part that mattered most. The youngest actor whispered that she had felt the storm disappear around her. Her words (11) ____ what I had learned: a sound effect was there to serve the story, not (12) ____ it. I had spent the first rehearsal trying to be (13) ____. By the last, I was listening. The curtain had not (14) ____ me from the play. It had given me another way to (15) ____ to it.

For our school radio play, I wanted the leading role. Instead, I was asked to produce the sound effects. I took the decision as a (1) ____: someone else would receive the applause while I stayed behind a curtain. At the first rehearsal, I barely listened to the actors. When rain was mentioned, I shook a tin of dry peas without waiting for the director's (2) ____. The noise drowned out a crucial line.
Afterwards, the youngest actor approached me. I expected a (3) ____, but she asked how I had made the rain. She had imagined real water falling into a bucket. Her curiosity (4) ____ me enough to explain the trick. As we experimented together, I noticed that a gentle movement produced a shower, while a rapid one suggested a storm. The same tin could express different (5) ____.
At the next rehearsal, I followed the script with a pencil. Rather than interrupting every mention of weather, I waited for a (6) ____ in the dialogue. This time, the rain seemed to belong to the scene. The director asked me to make it gradually fade as the character's fear (7) ____.
On performance day, the tin slipped from my hand just before my final cue. I caught it, but the peas had spilled. For a second, I (8) ____. Then I remembered the sheet of thin paper beside me. I rubbed it softly and (9) ____ the missing sound. Nobody in the audience saw the change.
At the end, the actors invited the crew forward. I was pleased, but the public (10) ____ was no longer the part that mattered most. The youngest actor whispered that she had felt the storm disappear around her. Her words (11) ____ what I had learned: a sound effect was there to serve the story, not (12) ____ it. I had spent the first rehearsal trying to be (13) ____. By the last, I was listening. The curtain had not (14) ____ me from the play. It had given me another way to (15) ____ to it.

questions.material:
I had captained our chess team for two years, so being named a reserve for the next match hurt. The coach said that recent results, not past titles, had guided her (1) ____. I nodded, though I privately considered the choice (2) ____.
During practice, I recorded the moves of Arun, a younger player who had only started learning chess the previous year. At first I wrote them down (3) ____, giving each position little thought. Then I saw him leave a piece apparently unprotected. I reached across to warn him, but the coach stopped me. Players had to make their own decisions. Arun's opponent took the piece, and two moves later Arun won. What I had taken for carelessness was a deliberate (4) ____.
Afterwards, Arun asked whether my notes showed the point at which his plan had become visible. He was not asking for (5) ____; he wanted a record that could help him improve. We studied the moves together. I found a weakness in a different line of play, and he spotted one in mine. The discussion became an (6) ____ rather than a lesson delivered by the older captain.
On match morning, one player fell ill. The coach asked me to take his (7) ____. My first response was relief, followed by a familiar urge to (8) ____ that I deserved my old position. Before we started, Arun handed me the notebook. Beside my earlier game, he had marked a safer response to an attack. I used that idea when a similar position (9) ____ and managed a draw.
Our team won narrowly. I could have treated the result as a personal (10) ____, but the notebook made that impossible. The useful suggestion had come from the player I had initially (11) ____. Later, I asked to keep recording games even when I was selected to play. Being a reserve had forced me to (12) ____ a strength that winning alone had hidden: I could learn from someone with less (13) ____. I still wanted to earn my place. What changed was my understanding of how to (14) ____ it. Protecting a title mattered less than remaining (15) ____ to advice.

Our costume club was making jackets for a school play. I had drawn a neat design with hidden pockets and wanted every jacket to look (1) ____. When a performer named Lena asked for an extra opening in her pocket, I refused. Any visible difference, I thought, would (2) ____ the design.
Lena did not argue. She asked me to watch a rehearsal before I made a final (3) ____. In one scene, she had to pass a letter to another character without turning towards him. Wearing my sample jacket, she repeatedly (4) ____ for the opening. Her hand caught in the lining, and the pause broke the flow of the scene.
Only then did she show me why she had asked for a change. An earlier wrist injury limited how far she could turn her hand. She could perform the movement comfortably with a wider side opening. The problem was not a lack of (5) ____; she had practised far longer than I realised. My jacket was demanding a movement that she could not comfortably make.

options.text: A. Purchase specialist equipment.
B. Complete a course with homework.
C. Buy an annual museum membership.
D. Reserve a place online.

questions.material:
Northgate Museum welcomes families to explore objects and the stories around them. All four programmes are free, but every family must reserve a place online before taking part. A reservation applies to the named session; it is not a general museum membership. Adults take part with their children, and no previous knowledge of the collections is needed. Read the four descriptions before choosing.

A1

Object Weekends
Designed for visitors of all ages, these sessions run on selected weekends throughout the year. A museum guide brings out an everyday object and asks how it might have been used. Visitors can compare materials, try a simple construction activity and talk with staff. Each weekend has a different topic; it is not a weekly course with homework.

A2

Small Discoverers
This programme is specifically designed for families with children aged 0–5. At the reserved session, adults and children move between low activity stations, exploring a theme through objects, picture books and play. Families may choose their order of activities after arrival. They still need the advance reservation required above; flexible movement does not mean unbooked admission.

A3

One Object, Many Questions
Held once each month, this programme is designed for families with children aged 3–8. A museum educator uses several items from the collection to introduce that month’s question. Families make or compare something together, and an invited maker sometimes joins the discussion. The activities take place in the museum’s learning room.

A4

Collections at Home
This online session is for families joining from home. It is held once each month and led by museum educators, with no visiting maker scheduled. Families use ordinary household items to explore a collection-related idea. A short materials list is sent after booking; specialist equipment is not needed. The aim is shared exploration rather than producing an identical object in every home.

options.text: A. Her printed pages were always delivered to another library.
B. The printer accepted only one paper size.
C. The price display changed before she could finish reading it.
D. Staff refused to explain any of the charges.

questions.material:
B1

When visitor Lena started using the self-service printing desk at fictional Hillcross Library, choosing the right charge was more difficult than collecting the pages. Several prices were displayed on a screen that changed before she had finished reading. Lena, who was learning the local language, usually asked staff to repeat the information and worried that she was delaying the queue.

Library assistant Dev noticed that she returned on the same afternoon each week. He could have selected the usual settings for her without asking, but he realised that a familiar order was not necessarily the order she wanted that day. Instead, he asked whether a small written list of the choices would help. Lena said it would, provided she could keep the list beside her while using the machine.

Dev prepared a plain card showing the current page sizes and charges. He checked it with his supervisor and asked Lena to point out anything unclear. options.text: A. Why all local collections should use workshop labels.
B. How to remove personal stories from a history room.
C. Why wooden handles are difficult to manufacture.
D. How the purpose of a catalogue can shape its categories.

questions.material:
C1

Two catalogues in the fictional town of Fenwick list many of the same objects but place them under different headings. The repair workshop groups a wooden handle with other tool parts. The local history room places a similar handle beside objects from an old kitchen. Neither arrangement is simply a careless version of the other: each was developed to answer a different kind of question.

The workshop’s system grew from practical requests. A worker looking for something to fit a damaged tool needed to compare size, shape and function quickly. Grouping parts by the work they could do was useful. The history room, by contrast, collected accounts of how objects had been used by particular households. Its visitors often wanted to reconstruct a setting or a period, so keeping related stories together made sense.

The difference became troublesome when the two organisations began sharing records. A volunteer searching one familiar category assumed that an object absent from it was absent from the collection. In fact, it appeared under another heading. The difficulty came from treating a category as a natural property of an object rather than as a choice made for a purpose.

The teams described this divergence as a movement towards different arrangements. They did not erase one catalogue and force every user into the other. Instead, they added short explanations and links between related entries. A handle could be found through its role as a part or through its place in a household account. The new links changed access without claiming that the two perspectives had become identical.

This fictional example illustrates why exchanging information requires more than copying labels. Users need to know what question a category helps answer and what it may leave out. A common access guide can make different systems easier to use while preserving useful distinctions. Difference, in this case, is neither a reason to stop cooperating nor evidence that one group thinks better than the other.

options.text: A. The lifetime cost of replacing library buildings.
B. Whether readers preferred printed books to digital copies.
C. Correct book-routing decisions under a time limit.
D. The safety of self-driving vehicles on public roads.

questions.material:
D1

Could a combination of people and software sort returned books more effectively than either working alone? An invented study at Orley Training Centre compared three decision conditions in a library simulation. It examined correct routing decisions under a time limit, not the safety of real transport systems or the value of every form of artificial intelligence.

Thirty adults were randomly assigned to three equal groups. All saw the same list of returned books, shelf positions and temporary closures. In the manual-only condition, participants planned routes using the printed information. In the automatic-only condition, they accepted a scheduling tool’s routes without changing them. In the combined condition, they could review the tool’s suggestions and correct them using the closure notices. Everyone received the same practice task and worked for the same period.

The combined group completed the most correct routes on average. The tool rapidly arranged ordinary items, while participants sometimes noticed a closure that its stored plan had missed. The manual group spent more time on routine ordering. The automatic group produced routes quickly but retained some routes through closed areas. Speed alone would therefore have given an incomplete picture of success.

These findings came from one comparison of three conditions, not from three separately described experiments. They suggest that, for this task and tool, human review and automated organisation could complement one another. They do not show that a combined system always wins. If every closure were already represented accurately in the tool, the balance might differ.

Researcher Bea Lin argues that future trials should vary the notices, time available and participants’ experience. Training would also matter: being allowed to override a suggestion is different from knowing when an override is justified. The centre plans to examine those questions before recommending any workplace use. Its immediate lesson is to evaluate the particular division of work, rather than to assume that adding software automatically removes the need for judgement.

D1

Could a combination of people and software sort returned books more effectively than either working alone? An invented study at Orley Training Centre compared three decision conditions in a library simulation. It examined correct routing decisions under a time limit, not the safety of real transport systems or the value of every form of artificial intelligence.

Thirty adults were randomly assigned to three equal groups. All saw the same list of returned books, shelf positions and temporary closures. In the manual-only condition, participants planned routes using the printed information. In the automatic-only condition, they accepted a scheduling tool’s routes without changing them. In the combined condition, they could review the tool’s suggestions and correct them using the closure notices. Everyone received the same practice task and worked for the same period.

The combined group completed the most correct routes on average. The tool rapidly arranged ordinary items, while participants sometimes noticed a closure that its stored plan had missed. The manual group spent more time on routine ordering. The automatic group produced routes quickly but retained some routes through closed areas. Speed alone would therefore have given an incomplete picture of success.

These findings came from one comparison of three conditions, not from three separately described experiments. They suggest that, for this task and tool, human review and automated organisation could complement one another. They do not show that a combined system always wins. If every closure were already represented accurately in the tool, the balance might differ.

Researcher Bea Lin argues that future trials should vary the notices, time available and participants’ experience. Training would also matter: being allowed to override a suggestion is different from knowing when an override is justified. The centre plans to examine those questions before recommending any workplace use. Its immediate lesson is to evaluate the particular division of work, rather than to assume that adding software automatically removes the need for judgement.

questions.material:
The fictional Citywheel Museum offers four ways for families to explore movement, making and everyday life. All four programmes are free, but every family must reserve a place online before taking part. Booking confirms one session rather than a place on a continuing course. The advertised age group describes the programme’s intended audience, so check the description as well as the title before reserving.

A1

Routes and Stories
These sessions welcome visitors of all ages on selected public-holiday weekends. A guide uses objects from the transport collection to begin conversations about ordinary journeys. Families can make a simple route model and compare their ideas with other groups. Topics change between sessions; attending an earlier event is not a requirement for joining a later one.

A2

Tiny Tracks
A programme specifically designed for families with children aged 0–5, Tiny Tracks combines a short picture-book introduction with playful exploration of objects and materials. Children take part with an accompanying adult. Once admitted to the reserved session, a family can move between activities at its own pace. This flexibility concerns the activities, not whether a booking is required.

A3

City Pieces
Once each month, an educator leads this programme for families with children aged 3–8. Participants compare several collection objects connected to that month’s theme, then build or draw together. A visiting designer sometimes demonstrates a technique. This session is held in the museum studio, and adults are expected to join in rather than leave children there.

A4

Window Workshop
An online gathering for families joining from home, Window Workshop takes place once each month. Museum educators suggest a way to explore a collection theme using materials commonly found at home. There is no scheduled visiting designer. Families receive a preparation note after booking and can choose how to adapt the activity to their available space.

options.text: A. The library had stopped accepting his borrowing card.
B. The staff trolley was already full of other visitors’ bags.
C. He had to manage his books and bag while one arm was in a sling.
D. His reserved books had been sent to another branch.

questions.material:
B1

At the fictional Berrin Library, regular borrower Tomas usually collected reserved books from a high counter. One week he arrived with his arm in a sling and discovered that managing a heavy bag while reaching for the books was awkward. He asked assistant Nila to set them down while he found his card. What happened next began with a question rather than a guess.

Nila did not assume that Tomas wanted someone else to choose or carry everything for him. She asked where he would like the books placed. He pointed to an empty trolley beside the counter. With the books there, he could check the titles and arrange his bag without balancing the whole pile against his body. He thanked her for giving him time instead of completing the transaction over his head.

The trolley had previously been kept behind the desk for staff returns. Nila asked the supervisor whether one could remain in front during busy periods. Before changing the arrangement, she tried two positions with Tomas so that it would not block the path or prevent someone reaching the counter. His suggestion was to keep it beside the lower end, where a visitor could ask to use it.

The following weeks showed that the change was useful to other borrowers too: one was sorting books for several family members, and another needed to put down a bulky bag. Staff still asked before moving anyone’s belongings. A convenient surface did not mean that all visitors wanted the same help, or that the library knew why each person found it useful.

Tomas later wrote a short message thanking Nila. “I asked for somewhere to put the books, and she listened to the somewhere,” he said. Nila describes the trolley as ordinary equipment finally being used from a visitor’s point of view. The library has not solved every access problem, but it has changed a routine by paying attention to a specific request. That, for her, is a practical part of welcoming people rather than an exceptional act of rescue.

options.text: A. Different definitions can make similarly labelled figures misleading to compare.
B. Why workshop staff should replace desk staff.
C. How to make all customers collect repairs on the same day.
D. Why accurate records are unnecessary in planning.

questions.material:
C1

When two teams report different completion times for the same kind of task, it is tempting to decide immediately that one works faster. A fictional repair centre discovered why that conclusion can be premature. Its desk team and workshop team both used the heading “time to completion”, but the two clocks did not begin at the same event.

The desk team measured from the moment a customer handed in an object until it was collected. Its figure included waiting for a part and waiting for the customer to return. The workshop team measured only the time between starting the repair and finishing the work. That shorter period answered a useful question about active work, but it was not a measurement of the customer’s entire wait.

The distinction emerged at a planning meeting. A manager compared the totals and asked why the desk was so slow. Desk staff pointed out that they did not perform the repairs whose timing appeared in the workshop column. Nor could they control when a customer came back. The numbers had been gathered carefully, yet their shared heading invited a comparison that the definitions did not support.

For that purpose, the measures were incompatible: they could not be treated as equivalent descriptions of the same interval. The centre did not discard either record. It renamed the columns, wrote a start and end event beside each one, and added separate waiting stages. A reader could then ask about active repair time or about overall service time without confusing the two.

questions.material:
D1

A fictional packing workshop has tested whether workers using a planning tool should be allowed to revise its instructions. The tool assigned small items to boxes, taking account of size but sometimes failing to recognise a newly added instruction to keep two items apart. The study compared one task under three conditions, not the general merits of all warehouse software.

Thirty-six adult volunteers were randomly allocated to equal groups. Everyone received the same order lists, item descriptions and separation notices. In the human-only condition, participants made a packing plan without the tool. In the tool-only condition, they followed its proposed plans without revision. In the reviewed-tool condition, they could examine and change a proposal before completing each order. All groups had equal practice and the same working period.

The reviewed-tool group completed the largest number of correct orders on average. The tool reduced some routine arranging, while human reviewers noticed separation notices that its stored template had missed. The human-only group often produced valid plans but completed fewer orders in the time. The tool-only group worked quickly, but some completed boxes failed the separation requirement. The researchers counted correct orders rather than treating the fastest completion as automatically best.

The comparison suggests that a particular combination of routine organisation and informed checking can be useful. It does not establish a permanent advantage for every mixed system. Better data in a later tool, different orders or inexperienced reviewers could change the outcome. The study also did not measure fatigue over a full working week.

Project lead Sora Pell says that future training should help reviewers understand why they accept or change a suggestion. A worker who clicks approval without reading the notice is not performing the role tested here. Before recommending workplace use, the team wants trials with more varied tasks and tools. It describes the result as a question about designing the division of work, rather than a reason to remove people from the process.

B. Completion of all the weekend sessions.

questions.material:
Explore the fictional Harbour Cabinet Museum with a programme that suits your family. All four programmes are free, but every family must reserve a place online before taking part. A confirmation message gives the session details and anything simple to bring. The programme descriptions below state their intended audiences and locations; a flexible activity format does not cancel the advance-booking rule.

A1

Harbour Clues
For visitors of all ages, Harbour Clues runs on selected weekends during the year. Families examine collection objects and consider what each might reveal about daily life beside the harbour. Guides offer short demonstrations and invite questions. Different weekends use different objects, so families can join a single session without following a fixed sequence of lessons.

A2

First Finds
First Finds is specifically designed for families with children aged 0–5. An educator introduces one theme through picture books, objects and playful activities, with caregivers taking part alongside their children. Families can choose which activity to try first during their reserved session. Places are still reserved online beforehand; free choice within the session is not permission to arrive without booking.

A3

Discover Together
This museum-room programme for families with children aged 3–8 is offered once each month. Families compare a small selection of objects connected with that month’s theme and create their own response through making or drawing. A guest craft worker sometimes contributes a demonstration. The purpose is exploration together, not judging families against one model answer.

A4

At-Home Cabinet
For families joining from home, this educator-led online session is held once each month. Ordinary household objects help participants explore an idea linked to the museum collection. There is no scheduled guest craft worker. A preparation message is sent after booking, and alternatives are suggested if a family lacks one of the proposed materials.

questions.material:
B1

At the fictional Ashford Garden Centre, employee Rafi knew that customer Elin usually bought the same small tray of seedlings. On a busy morning, he began reaching for it as soon as he saw her. options.text: A. Why newcomers cannot learn workshop tasks.
B. How to make every instruction as long as possible.
C. Why experienced members should stop asking questions.
D. How instructions may rely on knowledge shared by their audience.

questions.material:
C1

A short instruction that works well for an experienced group may puzzle a newcomer. In a fictional community workshop, the phrase “check the edge” had been used for years. Long-serving members knew which edge, what to compare it with and whom to ask if it differed. A new member saw several edges and had no reason to know which comparison was intended.

The phrase developed during repeated work on the same kind of object. Members could point, demonstrate and ask questions while using it. Over time, some of that shared experience disappeared from the written instruction because the regular group no longer needed it stated. The words became shorter, but the knowledge required to use them did not disappear.

The difficulty became clear when the workshop offered sessions to visitors. A volunteer initially assumed that the newcomers were failing to pay attention. Watching them work changed that view. They were checking carefully, but not all were checking the same edge. Their actions followed reasonable interpretations of an instruction that depended on information they had not been given.

Much of the instruction’s meaning was implicit: experienced members understood it without finding it fully expressed in the words. To help visitors, the team added a named reference point, a simple comparison and a person to consult if unsure. It also kept a shorter reminder version for regular members. The two versions served different audiences without implying that one group was less capable of learning.

This example illustrates a problem of shared knowledge, not a reason to make every instruction as long as possible. Extra words can also obscure a useful direction if they add nothing relevant. The aim is to identify what a reader must know and decide which parts can reasonably be assumed. A change of audience may require an explanation that was unnecessary among people working together every week.

options.text: A. Customer satisfaction over several years.
B. Whether repair work should be stopped permanently.
C. The commercial price of all scheduling software.
D. Workable schedules under different planning arrangements.

questions.material:
D1

An invented project at the Roven Skills Institute examined repair-job scheduling under three decision arrangements. A planning tool could organise ordinary jobs quickly, but its stored estimates did not always reflect a newly reported shortage of a particular part. Researchers wanted to compare the arrangements in a defined exercise rather than assume that automation alone would improve a real repair business.

Thirty adult volunteers were assigned by a random draw to three equal groups. They all received the same job list, estimated repair times and part-shortage notices. The planner-only group arranged the work using those documents. The automatic-only group accepted the tool’s timetable without editing it. The joint-decision group examined the proposed timetable and could change it in response to the notices. Practice time and the total time allowed were identical.

The joint-decision group produced the most workable schedules on average. Its members used the tool to organise routine jobs and changed some entries after noticing that the required part was unavailable. The planner-only group generally noticed the shortages but spent longer constructing an initial timetable. The automatic-only group finished quickly yet retained some jobs that could not begin as scheduled. The result depended on counting workable plans, not just speed.

This was a single comparison involving three groups. It provided support for combining this tool with informed review under the exercise’s conditions. A different tool that incorporated shortages accurately might produce a different pattern. The study also did not show how trainees would perform after months of work or when a notice itself was incorrect.

Institute researcher Jon Vale emphasises that an opportunity to change a timetable is useful only if reviewers understand what a change affects. Training and clear responsibility would remain important in any later trial. The team therefore plans to vary the task and the reliability of the information before drawing workplace conclusions. For now, the finding concerns a particular partnership between routine organisation and human judgement, not the disappearance of either role.

options.text: A. An Automatic Timetable That Cannot Contain Errors.
B. Three Long-Term Studies Replace All Human Planners.
C. Combining a Planning Tool with Judgement: A Scheduling Test.
D. Why Repair Centres Should Stop Training Their Staff.

questions.material:
D1

An invented project at the Roven Skills Institute examined repair-job scheduling under three decision arrangements. A planning tool could organise ordinary jobs quickly, but its stored estimates did not always reflect a newly reported shortage of a particular part. Researchers wanted to compare the arrangements in a defined exercise rather than assume that automation alone would improve a real repair business.

Thirty adult volunteers were assigned by a random draw to three equal groups. They all received the same job list, estimated repair times and part-shortage notices. The planner-only group arranged the work using those documents. The automatic-only group accepted the tool’s timetable without editing it. The joint-decision group examined the proposed timetable and could change it in response to the notices. Practice time and the total time allowed were identical.

The joint-decision group produced the most workable schedules on average. Its members used the tool to organise routine jobs and changed some entries after noticing that the required part was unavailable. The planner-only group generally noticed the shortages but spent longer constructing an initial timetable. The automatic-only group finished quickly yet retained some jobs that could not begin as scheduled. The result depended on counting workable plans, not just speed.

This was a single comparison involving three groups. It provided support for combining this tool with informed review under the exercise’s conditions. A different tool that incorporated shortages accurately might produce a different pattern. The study also did not show how trainees would perform after months of work or when a notice itself was incorrect.

Institute researcher Jon Vale emphasises that an opportunity to change a timetable is useful only if reviewers understand what a change affects. Training and clear responsibility would remain important in any later trial. The team therefore plans to vary the task and the reliability of the information before drawing workplace conclusions. For now, the finding concerns a particular partnership between routine organisation and human judgement, not the disappearance of either role.

questions.material:
A1

Bramble Shore Partnership — Shore Crew Leader

The fictional Bramble Shore Partnership invites applications for a paid youth fieldwork placement. The crew combines practical conservation with learning to record changes along a shore. Leaders work alongside site staff rather than directing the organisation’s national activities.

Key duties

Each leader guides 10–15 high-school students in teamwork, simple path maintenance and careful observation. The leader also keeps attendance records, checks equipment and reports concerns to site staff. A placement includes administrative work as well as practical sessions.

Schedule

The placement has two phases: spring (March–May 2027), Tuesday to Saturday; summer (June–August 2027), Monday to Friday. Leaders work 40 hours per week in either phase. The change of season changes the regular working days, not the weekly hours.

Location

Bramble Shore Reserve, beside the fictional town of Easthaven.

Qualifications

Applicants must be at least 21 on the first working day and hold a current driving licence held for at least 3 years; exactly three years satisfies that minimum. Applicants must be able to lift 40 pounds and work outdoors. Current CPR and outdoor first-aid certificates are required before field duties; training to obtain them is available before the placement. Previous conservation work and project leadership are preferred, not compulsory.

Compensation

$750 per week, paid every 2 weeks. The payment for two ordinary weeks is $1500 before deductions. The placement includes staff training; this is a fictional notice, not an actual offer of employment.

Work challenges

Sessions take place outdoors, where wind, wet ground and insects can change the working conditions. Leaders sometimes carry a field pack for several miles and must adjust a planned activity when site staff identify a problem. The post requires positive cooperation with people of different ages; it is not a desk-only appointment.

options.text: A. A controlled study of volunteers’ health.
B. A town-wide clock replacement competition.
C. A plan to sell all repaired objects.
D. A newsletter appeal for residents’ repair skills.

questions.material:
B1

A clock on a community-hall wall used to stop at the same minute every afternoon. At the fictional Bramble Repair Circle, an older volunteer brought it to a table where a teenager was learning to record faults. They did not immediately replace the clock. First they compared what happened when it was standing upright and when it was tilted. The small task gave both people a reason to ask questions.

The circle began after a neighbourhood newsletter invited residents to offer repair skills for one afternoon a month. It has since added sewing, simple tool maintenance and a place to exchange notes about objects that need specialist attention. Repairs are free; voluntary donations pay for materials. The organisers would rather decline a repair they cannot complete responsibly than treat every object as proof of their success.

Volunteer Eli joined after moving into a nearby flat. “I knew the streets, but I had hardly spoken to anyone,” he says. Working beside other residents gave him a regular reason to return and helped him feel part of the neighbourhood. He describes a change in his own experience. The circle has not compared his wellbeing with a control group, and his comment is not presented as a measured health effect.

The organisers are attuned to the different ways people take part. When they notice that a noisy demonstration makes questions hard to hear, they move the discussion to a quieter table. A visitor who cannot stay for a whole session can leave a dated note with the object instead. These adjustments do not create a faster repair for every visitor, but they help people enter a conversation that might otherwise pass them by.

The clock now works, yet the organisers keep a photograph of the shared inspection rather than a count of minutes saved. The circle's value also lies in the relationships formed around an uncertain task. It gives people of different generations an opportunity to learn each other's methods, while accepting that some objects must still go elsewhere for repair.
