questions.material:
C1

Dividing household work into equal shares sounds straightforward until partners ask what a share contains. Does taking full responsibility for the washing balance taking full responsibility for the cooking? Or does fairness feel different when both partners take part in each task? A fictional survey report examines that distinction without assuming that equal total hours describe every feature of a division of work.

In one comparison, 100 couples reported sharing responsibility for each regular chore, while another 100 reported assigning different chores to different partners. The partners in both groups estimated roughly equal individual shares of their household's total work. In the shared-responsibility group, 60 couples described their arrangement as fair; in the separate-task group, 30 did so. Those proportions show an association in the surveyed groups, not the result of assigning couples to different arrangements experimentally.

One possible explanation is that shared responsibility encourages partners to discuss details that a simple list of assigned jobs leaves invisible. Another runs in the opposite direction: couples who already communicate well may be more likely to choose shared responsibility. The report cannot decide between those directions from this comparison. It also does not claim that one arrangement suits every household or that equal hours are irrelevant.

A “grass is greener” effect offers another possibility. If you never prepare the food before cooking, washing a few plates may seem like the only demanding part of the evening. An unfamiliar job can look easier because you see its result but miss its preparation. As an outside researcher in this fictional report puts it, “A task can look lighter when you never have to prepare for it.” Actually doing the work may reveal effort that an observer had underestimated.

The report therefore combines a difference in reported fairness with several possible interpretations. It invites closer investigation of how partners understand one another's work. It does not convert the observed association into a proven recipe for a happier relationship.

options.text: A. Explore designs beyond a human hand’s form.
B. Interpret every object’s purpose through touch.
C. End physical testing after successful simulation.
D. Reproduce the human form exactly.

questions.material:
D1

A fictional engineering team has built a six-fingered robotic hand that can work both while attached to an arm and while moving independently across a table. The project explores whether changing the familiar shape of a hand can expand what a small machine does. Its demonstrations use lightweight objects in a controlled setting, rather than a finished product working in people's homes.

“We wanted to question the shape of a hand, not just copy its outline,” says the project leader. The fingers can bend backwards as well as forwards, allowing contact on either side of the palm. This feature makes the design different from a straightforward imitation of a human hand. It does not mean that the machine understands every object it touches or can carry an unlimited load.

To compare designs, the team used a search algorithm that combined features, simulated a task and retained better-performing combinations for another round. The process generated several candidates for physical testing. A good simulated result did not remove the need to test joints, balance and grip on the actual prototype. The algorithm helped explore design possibilities; it was not evidence that the machine learned every new job without guidance.

When attached to the arm, the hand could hold a light container against one side of its palm while securing a second object against the other. After detaching, it moved most steadily on four supporting fingers while using the remaining two to carry an object. In another arrangement, five fingers supported it and one carried a lighter item. The two arrangements used the same six fingers, with different roles, rather than extra fingers appearing during a task.

A later version might inspect narrow equipment spaces that a larger robot cannot enter. The team is also interested in whether such a design could eventually become a human-operated assistive hand. That possibility would require research into how a person could control and interpret movements unlike those of an ordinary hand. The report treats it as a question for further work, while presenting the current design as a useful challenge to familiar assumptions.

questions.material:
A1

Kestrel Grove Association — Grove Crew Leader

The fictional Kestrel Grove Association is recruiting leaders for a youth conservation crew. Its spring and summer placement gives high-school students experience of working on a shared outdoor site. Site specialists decide which areas can be used; leaders help students carry out the agreed tasks.

Key duties

A leader supervises 10–15 high-school students, teaches clear recording habits and supports teamwork during sign maintenance and habitat observation. Keeping the attendance list, checking borrowed tools and communicating with site specialists are regular duties. The leader remains part of the working crew.

Schedule

The placement has two phases: spring (March–May 2027), Tuesday to Saturday; summer (June–August 2027), Monday to Friday. Leaders work 40 hours per week in either phase. The change of season changes the regular working days, not the weekly hours.

Location

Kestrel Grove Field Centre, outside the fictional town of Norwick.

Qualifications

Applicants must be at least 21 on the first working day and hold a current driving licence held for at least 3 years; exactly three years satisfies that minimum. Applicants must be able to lift 40 pounds and work outdoors. Current CPR and outdoor first-aid certificates are required before field duties; training to obtain them is available before the placement. Previous conservation work and project leadership are preferred, not compulsory.

Compensation

$750 per week, paid every 2 weeks. The payment for two ordinary weeks is $1500 before deductions. The placement includes staff training; this is a fictional notice, not an actual offer of employment.

Work challenges

Activities involve uneven paths, changing temperatures and occasional contact with insects or irritating plants. A field pack may have to be carried for several miles. Leaders need to change an activity when conditions require it and communicate respectfully with students and staff. Most sessions are practical outdoor work rather than classroom lectures.

options.text: A. A laboratory promising to test every repaired bag.
B. A notice inviting shared objects and repair skills.
C. A shop requiring purchases before offering advice.
D. A teenager’s paid course outside the group.

questions.material:
B1

At a fictional repair afternoon in Norwick, a schoolbag lay open beside a tray of zips and buckles. Its owner expected a volunteer to take it away and return it repaired. Instead, the volunteer invited the owner to describe when the zip caught and asked a younger helper to record the result of a short test. The repair became a shared investigation rather than an invisible service.

The Norwick Patch Group started when a local noticeboard asked residents to bring both worn objects and skills they could share. The first meeting occupied one table. Now the group offers fabric repairs, a small tool desk and short demonstrations led by residents. Nobody has to buy a replacement object to attend. The service is free, with optional donations helping to cover materials and room costs.

Mina began volunteering after leaving a job with regular contact with customers. She missed those everyday conversations. At the repair table, she found she could explain a familiar method while hearing about the different ways people used their belongings. “I look forward to recognising people at the next meeting,” she says. This is her account of renewed contact, not a measured claim that volunteering changes everybody's mental or physical health.

The group is resourceful when a repair cannot be completed immediately. After a visitor brought a bag with a missing part, members used an unused sample to demonstrate the fitting and drew a simple diagram to take away. They did not pretend the sample was a permanent replacement. Finding a workable way to help mattered more than appearing to finish every job. They also keep a list of local specialists for tasks beyond the volunteers' experience.

Some visitors return with an object; others return to show how they used a suggestion. The organisers welcome both. A teenager who once wrote labels now leads a short session with an older member beside her. What the group passes on is more than a technique for fixing a zip: people learn whom they can ask, what they can contribute and when an uncertain repair needs another pair of eyes.

options.text: A. Equal fairness proportions under both arrangements.
B. Unequal total personal shares under separate tasks.
C. An experimentally imposed change of arrangements.
D. A higher fairness proportion under shared responsibility.

questions.material:
C1

An equal number of household tasks need not produce an equal sense of fairness. One task may involve noticing supplies, planning a sequence and finishing it; another may become visible only when someone points it out. A fictional survey asks whether couples feel differently about shared responsibility for each chore and separate ownership of different chores. It examines that distinction rather than treating a task count as a complete description of domestic work.

Researchers compared two groups of 100 couples. In one, partners shared responsibility across their regular chores; in the other, they assigned particular chores to particular partners. Both groups reported roughly equal personal shares of their household's total weekly work. 50 couples in the first group described the division as fair, compared with 25 in the second. The larger proportion did not come from a controlled change imposed by the researchers. It came from people reporting arrangements they already used.

Shared responsibility might encourage conversations about the parts of a job that otherwise remain unseen. But an existing habit of cooperation might also lead couples to share chores in the first place. The report treats these as different possible directions of explanation. The survey cannot demonstrate that changing the chore arrangement would produce the reported difference for a particular couple.

There may also be a “grass is greener” effect. A person who never organises the laundry may see only a neat pile of clothes and imagine a simpler job than clearing the kitchen. Sorting, checking labels and remembering a collection time can disappear from that view. A researcher not involved in the fictional survey comments, “Finishing a job is only the visible end of the work it involves.” Doing an unfamiliar chore could make its hidden demands easier to appreciate, although that possible mechanism was not separately tested here.

The findings are useful as a starting point for examining how fairness is understood. They compare reports under two arrangements and consider explanations that another study could test. They do not show that a numerical balance of hours is worthless or that there is one scientifically settled household routine for everyone.

questions.material:
D1

A six-fingered hand in a fictional robotics laboratory can leave its mechanical arm, cross a table and bring back a small object. The team designed it to test how one device might combine grasping with independent movement. It has been demonstrated with light objects on a prepared surface. Those demonstrations are an initial design study, not a record of a device working reliably in factories or as part of a human body.

“A hand-shaped machine need not inherit all the restrictions of a human hand,” the designer explains. The fingers bend towards either side of the palm, rather than closing in only one familiar direction. This gives the hand two useful gripping surfaces. The team is exploring the consequences of that difference, not claiming that an unfamiliar shape automatically improves every task.

The design search used a genetic algorithm: simulated combinations were compared on a set of tasks, and stronger candidates supplied features for the next round. The team then built versions to test physically. A shape that looked balanced in simulation could still perform poorly when a joint behaved differently on the table. Design search and physical checking therefore had separate roles in the process.

With the hand connected to the arm, two light objects could be secured on opposite sides of the palm. When disconnected, it could use four fingers to support movement and two to hold an object. For a lighter load it could instead walk on five fingers and reserve one for carrying. Changing the roles did not increase the total beyond six. The team also checked the connection before allowing the arm to lift a returned object, rather than treating arrival beside the arm as successful attachment.

The researchers see a possible use in checking narrow spaces around equipment. A version controlled by a person might also be considered for an assistive hand, but how a user would command and interpret these movements remains unresolved. The report distinguishes what the prototype did from what later designs might do. Its interest lies in expanding a design question while keeping the need for further tests in view.

questions.material:
A1

Reedbank Habitat Group — Habitat Crew Leader

The fictional Reedbank Habitat Group offers a paid placement leading young people in conservation work. The crew observes seasonal changes and helps maintain an outdoor learning area. Leaders coordinate daily work with site staff and make sure the student group can understand the purpose of each agreed task.

Key duties

Leaders guide 10–15 high-school students in teamwork, record keeping and straightforward site-maintenance tasks. They prepare the equipment list, keep attendance records and pass observations to the site team. Supporting a safe working routine and including quieter members are part of the role.

Schedule

The placement has two phases: spring (March–May 2027), Tuesday to Saturday; summer (June–August 2027), Monday to Friday. Leaders work 40 hours per week in either phase. The change of season changes the regular working days, not the weekly hours.

Location

Reedbank Outdoor Learning Site, near the fictional town of Alden.

Qualifications

Applicants must be at least 21 on the first working day and hold a current driving licence held for at least 3 years; exactly three years satisfies that minimum. Applicants must be able to lift 40 pounds and work outdoors. Current CPR and outdoor first-aid certificates are required before field duties; training to obtain them is available before the placement. Previous conservation work and project leadership are preferred, not compulsory.

Compensation

$750 per week, paid every 2 weeks. The payment for two ordinary weeks is $1500 before deductions. The placement includes staff training; this is a fictional notice, not an actual offer of employment.

Work challenges

Field sessions may involve heat, rain, insects and uneven surfaces. Some routes require carrying a field pack for several miles. Leaders need to adapt a plan to site conditions and work constructively with students from varied backgrounds. Staff support is available, but applicants should expect physical outdoor work, not solely office administration.

questions.material:
B1

The first repaired object at a fictional Alden community event was not a machine but a loose chair cover. A resident who knew sewing asked another visitor to hold the cloth while they compared the seams. A child wrote a label explaining which edge needed attention. By the time the cover was fitted again, several people who had arrived separately had begun working as a small group.

The Alden Mend-and-Meet session grew from a local appeal for residents willing to share practical skills. It now includes simple fabric repairs, a place to check small wooden objects and a desk for advice about finding specialist help. Visitors are not charged. Optional donations cover thread, labels and other basic materials; the event is not intended to compete with a professional repair service or promise that every item can be restored.

Tomas, who volunteers at the wooden-object table, says the event changed how he spent an otherwise quiet Saturday. He had skills from a former job but few reasons to use them with other people. Explaining a repair gave him a reason to listen as well as talk. He now recognises more neighbours outside the hall. The organisers present this as one volunteer's account of connection, without claiming a measured change in health or a result guaranteed for other participants.

The sessions are deliberately inclusive. Newcomers can begin by writing labels, comparing photographs or simply observing before joining a repair. Organisers place chairs so a visitor can sit beside a table without having to demonstrate a skill first. Younger members sometimes read a diagram for an older visitor, while experienced sewers show them how to examine a seam. There is more than one way to contribute.

At the end of a session, the organisers ask what people learned from one another as well as which objects were repaired. A finished chair cover matters, but so does the exchange that helped finish it. The project offers a meeting place around practical questions, making connections between generations that a request for a repair alone might never have created.

options.text: A. Identical fairness proportions under both arrangements.
B. Unequal overall personal shares under separate tasks.
C. A higher fairness proportion under shared responsibility.
D. A causal effect established by random assignment.

questions.material:
C1

When partners discuss housework, the final list of assigned jobs can hide a difference in responsibility. One couple may split tasks so that each partner owns particular jobs. Another may share the planning and completion of each regular chore. A fictional research report compares those arrangements, asking about reported fairness while recognising that a balanced total of work does not describe every part of a household routine.

The report compared 100 couples using shared responsibility with 100 using separate task ownership. In both groups, partners estimated roughly equal individual shares of their household's total work. 40 couples in the shared group and 20 in the separate-task group said their arrangements were fair. The proportions differed, even though the reported total shares were similar. The researchers had observed existing routines; they had not randomly assigned the couples to new ones.

A shared approach could make partners discuss the less visible requirements of a task. Yet the causal direction could run the other way: people with an established habit of cooperation might be more likely to choose shared responsibility. Other differences between the groups might also matter. The report sets out these alternatives rather than presenting the comparison as proof that one change in routine would produce a particular result.

An unfamiliar chore may also benefit from a “grass is greener” impression. A partner who rarely organises meals may see cooking as a short activity at the stove, overlooking the search for ingredients and the planning around other commitments. An outside researcher in the account comments, “Seeing the result of a chore does not necessarily reveal its full burden.” Taking a turn at the work could make its demands clearer. That is a possible explanation to investigate, not an additional result already established by the comparison.

The report's contribution is to make a pattern and the questions behind it visible. It asks why different arrangements might feel fair, and what further evidence would help distinguish explanations. It does not offer a universal rule for assigning chores, or conclude that the amount of work people do has no bearing on fairness.

options.text: A. Guarantee practical success through a simulated grip.
B. Changing form can open new design possibilities.
C. Treat every ordinary hand movement as unnecessary.
D. Build human finger limits into every robot.

questions.material:
D1

In a fictional design project, a six-fingered robotic hand can grip an object while attached to an arm and can travel across a tabletop after being released. Its designers are studying how grasping and movement might fit within one device. The account describes controlled trials with light objects. It does not describe a commercial machine already operating in unpredictable working environments.

“The useful question is what a hand can do when its design is allowed to change,” says the designer. Instead of limiting the fingers to the familiar movement towards one side of a palm, the team gave them joints that bend backwards as well. The hand can therefore use both sides for holding objects. This departure from a human outline is a design opportunity, rather than a claim that every ordinary hand movement has become unnecessary.

The researchers used a genetic algorithm to explore combinations of finger lengths and joint movement. Simulated candidates were tested against selected tasks, and better-performing combinations were carried into later rounds. Physical prototypes still had to be checked. A simulated grip could fail when a real surface slipped, so the search procedure did not certify practical success or replace observations of the built hand.

On the arm, the prototype could hold a light object against each side of its palm at the same time. Off the arm, it moved steadily with four supporting fingers while two held a small load. It could also use five for support and one for a lighter object. In both cases the roles added up to the same six fingers. The report distinguishes moving close to an object from actually securing it; a promising route across the table was not automatically a successful carrying trial.

One possible application is inspection inside narrow equipment spaces. The designers also discuss a future hand operated by a human user, but that would require research into control and the user's interpretation of unfamiliar movements. No such interface has been validated in these trials. The report welcomes the broader design possibilities while leaving the proposed human application dependent on further work.

B. A Robotic Hand Tests New Ways to Grip and Move.
C. Routine Use of Inspection Hands Across Industry.
D. A Clinically Validated Human-Hand Replacement.

questions.material:
D1

In a fictional design project, a six-fingered robotic hand can grip an object while attached to an arm and can travel across a tabletop after being released. Its designers are studying how grasping and movement might fit within one device. The account describes controlled trials with light objects. It does not describe a commercial machine already operating in unpredictable working environments.

“The useful question is what a hand can do when its design is allowed to change,” says the designer. Instead of limiting the fingers to the familiar movement towards one side of a palm, the team gave them joints that bend backwards as well. The hand can therefore use both sides for holding objects. This departure from a human outline is a design opportunity, rather than a claim that every ordinary hand movement has become unnecessary.

The researchers used a genetic algorithm to explore combinations of finger lengths and joint movement. Simulated candidates were tested against selected tasks, and better-performing combinations were carried into later rounds. Physical prototypes still had to be checked. A simulated grip could fail when a real surface slipped, so the search procedure did not certify practical success or replace observations of the built hand.

On the arm, the prototype could hold a light object against each side of its palm at the same time. Off the arm, it moved steadily with four supporting fingers while two held a small load. It could also use five for support and one for a lighter object. In both cases the roles added up to the same six fingers. The report distinguishes moving close to an object from actually securing it; a promising route across the table was not automatically a successful carrying trial.

One possible application is inspection inside narrow equipment spaces. The designers also discuss a future hand operated by a human user, but that would require research into control and the user's interpretation of unfamiliar movements. No such interface has been validated in these trials. The report welcomes the broader design possibilities while leaving the proposed human application dependent on further work.

questions.material:
Choosing a Question You Can Investigate

An interesting research question is not always a manageable one. Before a school project begins, students need to consider both what they want to learn and how they could obtain evidence. The following steps offer a way to narrow an idea without losing its purpose.

Start with a question that matters to you

[1], so begin by writing down something you would like to understand better. If you wonder why a particular classroom stays cooler than another, your concern about comfort can provide a starting point. At this stage, you do not need a detailed plan or a promise that you will find a particular answer.

[2]

Once you have chosen a topic, specify what you would compare. For example, one student may want to compare temperatures in two rooms at the same time rather than record a vague impression of which room feels comfortable. The comparison should make clear what information would count as evidence.

Check whether your evidence would answer it

A method is useful only if its results are relevant to the question. [3]. A temperature record collected at different times, for instance, might mix a difference between rooms with a difference between mornings and afternoons. Merely collecting more numbers would not remove that uncertainty.

Check what you need to collect the evidence

After choosing a method, find out whether the necessary resources are available. [4], ask your science teacher how the equipment can be borrowed and used safely. If a project requires permission rather than equipment, contact the person responsible before collecting the information. These are two different needs, so do not treat asking permission as a substitute for checking a device.

[5]. Make a brief plan showing when you will collect the information and how you will compare the results. You may discover that your first question needs to be narrower. That is a useful revision, not a reason to hide evidence that fails to support your original expectation.

A. Return to the two-room example
B. Personal curiosity can give you a reason to keep investigating
C. If no equipment is needed
D. With these requirements settled, you can plan the investigation
E. Compare possible topics before choosing one
F. Identify a feature that you can compare
G. If it needs a measuring device

questions.material:
(1) ____ (open) in 1998, the prop cupboard behind our town theatre holds far more than spare hats. It is (2) ____ place where objects acquire new identities: a wooden box becomes a treasure chest, while a kitchen chair becomes a throne. Last month two (3) ____ (student) were invited to help prepare a display about this hidden part of theatre life.

Rather than arranging the objects by price, the pair chose (4) ____ (show) how the same item had appeared in different plays. A small card beside each object explains (5) ____ it was used for. The most popular object is an umbrella (6) ____ handle was repaired with bright blue tape. Visitors can compare a photograph of its first appearance with one taken ten years later.

The students described each change as (7) ____ (accurate) as they could. They also asked the theatre's (8) ____ (manage) for permission to include a broken crown. She agreed, because the damage revealed how many times it had been worn. Since the cupboard was rearranged in May, several local actors (9) ____ (offer) to contribute objects of their own. Each new contribution arrives with a short note, so visitors know not only what an object is, (10) ____ also why somebody decided to keep it.

(1) ____ (open) in 1998, the prop cupboard behind our town theatre holds far more than spare hats. It is (2) ____ place where objects acquire new identities: a wooden box becomes a treasure chest, while a kitchen chair becomes a throne. Last month two (3) ____ (student) were invited to help prepare a display about this hidden part of theatre life.

Rather than arranging the objects by price, the pair chose (4) ____ (show) how the same item had appeared in different plays. A small card beside each object explains (5) ____ it was used for. The most popular object is an umbrella (6) ____ handle was repaired with bright blue tape. Visitors can compare a photograph of its first appearance with one taken ten years later.

The students described each change as (7) ____ (accurate) as they could. They also asked the theatre's (8) ____ (manage) for permission to include a broken crown. She agreed, because the damage revealed how many times it had been worn. Since the cupboard was rearranged in May, several local actors (9) ____ (offer) to contribute objects of their own. Each new contribution arrives with a short note, so visitors know not only what an object is, (10) ____ also why somebody decided to keep it.

questions.material:
A useful exhibition label does more than give an object a name. It helps a visitor notice something worth examining. Before writing, decide what this particular object can help a visitor understand.

Begin with a reason to look

(1) ____, so start with a detail that makes the object worth a closer look. A repaired seam in an old bag, for example, can raise a question about how it was used. You do not need to tell the whole history in the opening line.

(2) ____

After choosing that detail, check which statements are supported by the records. A date written on a repair receipt may establish when the work was paid for, but not exactly when the bag was first used. Keep those two claims separate when describing the seam.

Return to the example

A confident sentence can hide a weak link. (3) ____. The receipt can support the payment date, while the earlier history remains uncertain. Saying so gives visitors a way to understand the limit rather than asking them to accept an unexplained conclusion.

Check the reproduction plan

Some labels include a photograph that belongs to someone outside the exhibition team. (4) ____, obtain the required reproduction permission before sending the label to the printer. If the team owns the image, check the internal record instead. These are different routes for establishing what may be printed.

(5) ____. Put the draft beside the object and ask a reader to use them together. If the reader cannot find the seam mentioned in the text, revise the wording or placement before deciding that the label is finished.

共享候选（两项不用）：

A. If the photograph belongs to an outside owner
B. Check what the evidence can support
C. If no photograph is being printed
D. A visible detail can give visitors a reason to pause
E. With the evidence and image rights checked, test the label in place
F. Go back to the repair receipt and the seam
G. Write the printer’s name in larger letters

questions.material:
(1) ____ (build) above an old apartment block, the shared drying terrace was once used by only a few residents. It is now (2) ____ place where neighbours often meet. A photograph taken before the recent changes shows two rusty (3) ____ (bench) and a row of empty plant pots. The residents chose (4) ____ (replace) the damaged seats before doing anything else.

At their first meeting, one neighbour demonstrated (5) ____ a folding chair could be stored flat against the wall: she released a small catch and lifted the seat. Another resident, (6) ____ flat faces the terrace, offered to check the furniture after heavy rain. Nobody wanted the roof to become a private garden that only a few people felt entitled to use.

The new rules were therefore written as (7) ____ (clear) as possible. The building's (8) ____ (manage) agreed to keep the access door open during the stated hours. Since the seats were installed in June, more families (9) ____ (use) the terrace while waiting for their washing to dry. Some bring a book; others simply sit quietly. The residents value the changes not only because the roof looks better, (10) ____ also because an ordinary household task now gives them a reason to speak to one another.

At their first meeting, one neighbour demonstrated (5) ____ a folding chair could be stored flat against the wall: she released a small catch and lifted the seat. Another resident, (6) ____ flat faces the terrace, offered to check the furniture after heavy rain. Nobody wanted the roof to become a private garden that only a few people felt entitled to use.

The new rules were therefore written as (7) ____ (clear) as possible. The building's (8) ____ (manage) agreed to keep the access door open during the stated hours. Since the seats were installed in June, more families (9) ____ (use) the terrace while waiting for their washing to dry. Some bring a book; others simply sit quietly. The residents value the changes not only because the roof looks better, (10) ____ also because an ordinary household task now gives them a reason to speak to one another.

B. If the workshop has already given final approval
C. Separate agreed facts from unfinished choices
D. A reader needs to know where to pick up the work
E. With those responsibilities clear, close the handover loop
F. Ask every reader to repeat the project’s entire history
G. If a client holds the final decision about colour

questions.material:
A workshop handover is useful only if the next person can continue the work without reconstructing every decision. A long account is not necessarily a helpful one. The following sequence offers a way to prepare a short, usable record.

Say what comes next

(1) ____, so begin with the action that the next person is expected to take. For example, write that three sample cards need checking before printing, rather than filling the first page with the history of the project. Background can follow when it explains a decision the reader needs to make.

(2) ____

Once the next action is clear, distinguish settled decisions from choices that are still open. A card's final size may already have been approved, while its colour is awaiting a trial print. Mark that difference instead of describing both as “almost finished”.

Examine the example again

Unclear status words can turn a request into an assumption. (3) ____. The reader needs to know that size requires no new decision, whereas the colour still needs checking. A short note can make that distinction more clearly than several cheerful sentences about progress.

Match approval to responsibility

Different choices may belong to different people. (4) ____, send the colour result to that person before approving the print run. If the workshop itself has final authority, record its own approval. Passing information on is not the same as acquiring the right to approve it.

(5) ____. Leave space for the next person to confirm what was received and record what they did. The handover then becomes a connection between two stages of work, rather than a document whose accuracy nobody checks after it is sent.

共享候选（两项不用）：

A. Return to the cards whose size is settled but whose colour is not
B. If the workshop has already given final approval
C. Separate agreed facts from unfinished choices
D. A reader needs to know where to pick up the work
E. With those responsibilities clear, close the handover loop
F. Ask every reader to repeat the project’s entire history
G. If a client holds the final decision about colour

(1) ____ (establish) beside a public library, a small printing workshop has become (2) ____ place for local groups to make posters. On the front desk stand three cardboard (3) ____ (box), labelled with different paper sizes. The workshop's founder decided (4) ____ (save) clean offcuts instead of throwing them away after each job.

A notice above the desk explains (5) ____ the offcuts can be used for. A visitor, (6) ____ daughter was making invitations, recently found enough matching pieces for a whole set. She said that being able to see the available sizes made planning easier. The workshop does not promise that the same colours will always be in stock; the contents change whenever a larger printing job is finished.

Volunteers measure each piece as (7) ____ (careful) as they can before sorting it. The workshop's (8) ____ (manage) keeps a separate tray for pieces too small for the labelled boxes. Since the system began in March, several local clubs (9) ____ (ask) for paper that would otherwise have been discarded. They value it not only because it costs nothing, (10) ____ also because the unexpected colours sometimes lead them towards a design they would never have planned in advance.

questions.material:
For years, Mara had photographed the old footbridge near her village. She liked the way its shape changed with the seasons. When a local exhibition invited residents to contribute, she decided to (1) ____ a series of her pictures.

At the exhibition meeting, a younger organiser suggested displaying only the most beautiful view. Mara initially (2) ____. A single polished photograph would be easier to arrange. But an older resident asked where the temporary crossing had been during a winter repair. Mara searched her collection and found no (3) ____ of it. She had avoided photographing anything that spoiled the familiar view.

The question made her reconsider the purpose of the exhibition. Was she presenting a bridge, or only the bridge she (4) ____ to remember? She returned to the river with a notebook and began asking people about their journeys across it.

Their accounts did not always (5) ____. One resident remembered the repair starting in November; another insisted it was December. Instead of choosing the more confident speaker, Mara (6) ____ both accounts and looked for dated notices. A notice showed that work had been announced in November but the crossing had closed in December. The two people had remembered different (7) ____ of the same event.

She also found a photograph in a neighbour's drawer. It showed the temporary crossing, but a child's face was clearly visible. The neighbour permitted Mara to examine the picture, not to (8) ____ it. She respected that limit and used a drawing of the crossing in the exhibition instead.

Preparing the display took longer than she had (9) ____. Each new conversation raised questions about something she had once regarded as obvious. Yet the extra work gave the photographs a richer (10) ____. They were no longer simply attractive views; they were connected to people's daily lives.

At the opening, visitors paused beside a panel explaining the two repair dates. Some added their own memories. Mara could not (11) ____ every detail, but she could show where each claim came from and what remained uncertain.

The organiser later asked what she had learned. "A good record needs more than a steady camera," Mara replied. "It needs (12) ____ to notice what your favourite view leaves out." She continued photographing the river, now paying attention to ordinary crossings as well as special light. Her project had (13) ____ from a collection of personal favourites into a shared investigation. For Mara, its value lay less in producing a (14) ____ picture than in giving others a reason to (15) ____ their own stories.

questions.material:
At sixty-eight, Mara still begins a workshop by placing a damaged shopping bag on the table. She treats it as an opportunity to ask why something has failed. Visitors sometimes expect her to display prizes, but she opens a notebook containing decades of experiments instead.

Mara first wanted to study design when she was seventeen. Her family's budget could not (1) ____ the tuition, so she took a factory job and (2) ____ formal study. The decision changed her timetable, not her interest. In the evenings, she repaired neighbours' bags and kept careful (3) ____ of every alteration: the date, the material and the result.

Her first attempt at a new handle looked attractive, but it (4) ____ after a few minutes of carrying groceries. Rather than blame the owner, Mara (5) ____ the damaged seam to see where the stitches had pulled apart. She kept the failed handle beside the next model, so she could compare them without relying on memory.

When a later design was ready, she took it to market traders and asked for (6) ____, especially comments about what still did not work. Some found the handles awkward; others said the bag was difficult to store. Their suggestions (7) ____ the next version. Mara replaced a costly metal part with a cloth loop, (8) ____ the cost while keeping the feature the traders wanted.

After retiring from paid work, she (9) ____ a small repair class. Pupils brought objects they might otherwise have thrown away. Mara showed her failed experiments as well as her finished work, choosing to (10) ____ mistakes rather than pretend they had never happened. She provided spare tools because buying equipment would have been too (11) ____ for some beginners.

The purpose was to (12) ____ others how to repair with what was available, not to advertise a new brand. Looking through the notebook, visitors could see that her (13) ____ had been gradual. No single page explained everything. Different problems had required different responses.

Mara did not claim that every old object could be saved. Sometimes she marked an attempt “not successful” and explained the (14) ____ of her method. What she valued most was (15) ____: the wish to keep asking what might work better, even after many years of trying.

At seventy-one, Lena still spends Saturday mornings at a chessboard, but she no longer welcomes newcomers as an (1) ____ trying to beat them across the table. She pulls a chair beside them and asks what they notice about the position. The aim is to understand their thinking before offering her own.

As a teenager, Lena learnt from books she (2) ____ from the public library. Tournament entry fees and long train journeys were beyond her (3) ____, so she played at home instead. Years later, a free local club gave her the opportunity to meet stronger players. Her first results were disappointing, and for a while she considered (4) ____ altogether.

A club member suggested that she write down the moves from one lost game. At first, she wanted to skip the embarrassing parts, but the written record made them impossible to (5) ____. She began to examine not only her final mistake but the earlier decisions that had made it likely. A lost game became a source of (6) ____ rather than a reason to avoid the board.

Lena continued to work full time, setting aside a small amount each month for travel. She chose a few events she could (7) ____ instead of entering every competition. Her improvement was (8) ____, built through repeated practice and review rather than a sudden run of victories. She never became a famous champion, but she grew less afraid of discussing a move she did not understand.

After retirement, the club (9) ____ her to help with beginners: “Would you like to lead a group?” She initially prepared long explanations, then discovered that new players often needed time to try a position for themselves. She learnt to (10) ____ her teaching, using shorter questions and waiting for answers. A quiet pupil was not necessarily an uninterested one; some were considering several possibilities.

Lena also asked the club to keep a set of boards that anyone could borrow. She remembered how lack of money had once (11) ____ her own choices. The extra boards would not make everyone equally skilled, but they would make the activity more (12) ____.

Today, a visitor might mistake her patience for a gift she had always possessed. Her notebooks tell a different story: frustration, corrections and plans that had to be (13) ____. She shares those pages openly, so learners know that uncertainty is part of learning. Her greatest (14) ____ now is not a higher place in a competition. It is seeing someone return after a difficult game, ready to (15) ____ again.

A1

Northbay Upper School certificate requirements

The following rules belong to an invented school. Students must meet all the requirements to receive its upper-school certificate.

Compulsory credits

4 credits in English (one credit in each of Years 9–12)

3 credits in mathematics (including at least one credit in Year 11 or 12)

3 credits in project courses from the three approved groups

2 credits in science

1 credit in community history

1 credit in local geography

1 credit in the arts

1 credit in health and physical education

1 credit in an additional language

0.5 credit in career studies

0.5 credit in civic participation

Optional credits

Students must earn 12 optional credits from approved courses. Up to 4 of these optional credits may come from approved partner-college courses; they are included, not added to the optional total.

Online learning

Students who entered Year 9 in September 2025 or later must complete at least 2 credits online. These online credits count within the compulsory or optional requirements above; they are not extra credits.

Literacy requirement

The literacy rule takes effect on 1 September 2026. Students graduating in 2026–2027 or later must satisfy the school’s literacy check as well as its credit requirements.

Community involvement

At least 40 hours of approved community activity are required. These hours are not course credits. Before beginning, students must:

check that the proposed activity meets the school’s approval rules;

consult the school’s list of approved and prohibited activities;

discuss the plan with a parent or guardian if they are under 18.

Students aged 18 or over must still verify that an activity qualifies, but the parent-or-guardian discussion rule does not apply to them.

options.text: A. All damage had been caused by volunteers entering unsafe areas.
B. The reserve’s young plants had become fully resistant to disturbance.
C. Some visitors had left the marked route near a damaged barrier.
D. The team had completed every repair the previous winter.

questions.material:
B1

During a winter inspection of the fictional Rellin Dune Reserve, volunteer leader Anya noticed fresh footprints beside a damaged path barrier. The marks mattered because visitors leaving the marked route could disturb the young plants the team was trying to protect. She recorded the location before touching anything. A photograph of an empty path would not have shown where the problem had begun.

Anya joined the reserve’s volunteer group eight years earlier, initially helping to label observations collected by more experienced members. She now coordinates visits, checks equipment and teaches new volunteers how to keep records that another person can understand. Strong wind and shifting sand often make the work uncomfortable, but the team avoids entering unsafe areas merely to complete a planned route.

Last autumn, volunteers dismantled an old barrier that had become unstable. They took its loose sections apart and removed them before installing a better-marked replacement. The task required more than enthusiasm: members had to identify which pieces were unsafe and carry them away without trampling the area they meant to protect. Anya asked the newer volunteers to observe the first section before working in pairs.

The reserve lies between two villages, whose teams once kept separate records of damaged signs. They now exchange dated notes and use the same location labels. A repair recorded by one team is therefore less likely to be mistaken for a new problem by the other. Anya regards this cooperation as part of conservation work itself, because repeated visits are of limited value if the information cannot be combined.

Recent checks have found fewer people leaving the path at that spot, although the team does not claim that a new barrier alone caused every change. Weather and visitor numbers vary too. The volunteers plan to continue observing and adjusting the route. Their work combines practical effort with careful judgement: noticing a problem, acting without creating another one, and leaving a record that others can use.

options.text: A. By giving the author’s childhood memory.
B. By defining a brain region.
C. By inviting the reader to imagine a preparation situation.
D. By reporting a large controlled experiment.

questions.material:
C1

Imagine preparing to explain a simple demonstration in front of a class. You can read your notes again, but you can also picture yourself lifting the first object, pausing for a question and moving to the next step. That imagined sequence is a kind of mental rehearsal. In this fictional example, it helps a presenter inspect a plan before carrying it out; it does not count as having performed the demonstration.

Presenter Mara tried the approach before a practice session. As she pictured the sequence, she realised that a question from the audience might arrive before she had put one object down. Her plan had left no hand free for the next one. She changed the order in her notes, then tested it with the actual objects. The useful point was the problem she had noticed, not a promise that imagining an action makes every detail physically possible.

After the session, Mara said that she had felt more prepared to begin. That was a report about her own experience. Nobody measured a change in her strength, recorded her brain activity or compared her performance with a large control group. It would therefore be unjustified to turn her comment into a general claim that mental rehearsal produces the same bodily effects as physical practice.

The approach can be understood as a way of asking more specific questions. “What happens after I lift this?” may reveal something that “Will I do well?” leaves vague. A musician could similarly picture a difficult transition before testing it on an instrument. A volunteer might mentally walk through a greeting and the first question a visitor is likely to ask. In each case, thinking identifies a possible issue; real conditions may still expose another one.

Mental rehearsal is most useful in this account when it leads back to observation and adjustment. An imagined audience may be quieter than the real class, and a step that seems smooth in thought may need physical practice. Mara’s experience suggests a modest role for imagination: it can make a plan available for inspection. It cannot certify success, replace every rehearsal or settle what another person will do.

options.text: A. A single sensor that also manufactures every replacement unit.
B. A change in an organism’s biological cells.
C. An unlimited supply of energy produced by the patch.
D. A controller using signals and the stored layout.

questions.material:
D1

A fictional materials project at Vey Institute has explored how a protective panel might coordinate small repairs. The model is inspired by the idea of parts responding to a local problem, but it is an engineered demonstration, not a study showing that an organism can regenerate or that a human injury can be treated.

The team built panels from small connected units and combined local sensing with a shared location code. In a trial, a sensor first detects a break in one unit’s outer layer. It then sends a location signal to neighbouring units. A controller checks that signal against the panel’s layout and guides a replacement patch towards the indicated gap. Only after the patch is aligned does a fastening step hold it in place. The sequence matters: attaching a patch before its position is checked could leave the original gap uncovered.

The researchers describe the controller as coordinating information, not as supplying the patch material or generating unlimited energy. Sensors, a stored layout, replacement material and the fastening process each play a different role. When a location code was deliberately left out of one trial, the system could signal that something was wrong without placing the patch correctly. Detecting damage was therefore not the same achievement as completing a repair.

questions.material:
A1

Rowan Upper School certificate requirements

The following rules belong to an invented school. Students must meet all the requirements to receive its upper-school certificate.

Compulsory credits

4 credits in English (one credit in each of Years 9–12)

4 credits in mathematics (including at least one credit in Year 11 or 12)

3 credits in project courses from the three approved groups

3 credits in science

1 credit in community history

1 credit in local geography

1 credit in the arts

1 credit in health and physical education

1 credit in an additional language

0.5 credit in career studies

0.5 credit in civic participation

Optional credits

Students must earn 10 optional credits from approved courses. Up to 3 of these optional credits may come from approved partner-college courses; they are included, not added to the optional total.

Online learning

Students who entered Year 9 in September 2024 or later must complete at least 2 credits online. These online credits count within the compulsory or optional requirements above; they are not extra credits.

Literacy requirement

The literacy rule takes effect on 1 October 2026. Students graduating in 2026–2027 or later must satisfy the school’s literacy check as well as its credit requirements.

Community involvement

At least 40 hours of approved community activity are required. These hours are not course credits. Before beginning, students must:

check that the proposed activity meets the school’s approval rules;

consult the school’s list of approved and prohibited activities;

discuss the plan with a parent or guardian if they are under 18.

Students aged 18 or over must still verify that an activity qualifies, but the parent-or-guardian discussion rule does not apply to them.

options.text: A. All of the wetland had been proved chemically polluted.
B. Volunteers had been asked to enter every inaccessible location.
C. The same person had been identified as the source of every item.
D. Discarded wrapping had gathered at an inlet beside a protected bank.

questions.material:
B1

At the fictional Aldercombe Wetland, conservation volunteer Mikel found a strip of packing material caught against an inlet screen after heavy rain. The team was trying to prevent discarded material from collecting along a protected bank. Instead of reporting the whole wetland as polluted, he noted exactly what he could see and where it had gathered. The observation was specific enough for another person to check.

Mikel first joined the team as a student labelling bags of collected litter. He now organises inspection rounds and helps new volunteers distinguish a recorded observation from a guess about its source. A photograph of wrapping does not, by itself, identify who discarded it or how far it travelled. The team removes material where permitted and refers inaccessible locations to the trained maintenance crew.

After a storm, an old observation platform was decommissioned. It was formally taken out of use because its supports needed assessment, and volunteers stopped recording from it. Rather than disguise the interruption as a complete series of observations, Mikel marked the missing dates. The team used another approved observation point while keeping its records separate from those made at the old platform.

Two local groups inspect different inlets. They now exchange dates, location codes and the categories used for collected material. A bag counted as one item by one group had previously been counted by its separate pieces by the other. Agreeing on a method made the records more comparable. It did not mean that the inlets received identical amounts of litter or that all material had the same source.

Recent rounds have found less loose wrapping at the first screen, but Mikel does not attribute that change to the volunteers alone. Water movement, rainfall and maintenance timing also vary. He values people who can return regularly, handle ordinary clearing work carefully and explain what their records do not establish. Conservation, for this team, includes keeping the wetland cleaner without making its evidence look more certain than it is.

He values people who can return regularly, handle ordinary clearing work carefully and explain what their records do not establish. Conservation, for this team, includes keeping the wetland cleaner without making its evidence look more certain than it is.

options.text: A. Through the author’s personal travel diary.
B. Through a list of measured brain responses.
C. Through a situation the reader is asked to imagine.
D. Through an official museum safety regulation.

questions.material:
C1

Suppose a new museum volunteer is about to explain an unfamiliar object to visitors. She may know several facts yet still be unsure how to begin. In a fictional training session, volunteer Isha tried picturing the first minute: where she would stand, what she would point to and which question a visitor might ask. The imagined scene helped make a vague worry more specific.

While rehearsing in thought, she noticed that her intended opening depended on a small mark visitors could not see from where she planned to stand. She moved the object during the real practice and tested the view with a partner. The imagined difficulty was useful because it led to a check. It was not evidence that a view imagined from one position must match the view another person actually has.

Afterwards, Isha reported feeling less uncertain about her first sentence. The account does not include a measurement of physical skill or a controlled comparison of visitor learning. Her change in confidence and the practical adjustment are different kinds of information. Neither establishes that imagining an explanation has the same effect on the body as delivering it, or that every visitor will now understand it.

Mental rehearsal in this account means running through a sequence from a particular point of view, then asking what might have been left out. A presenter can picture a transition between two ideas. A guide can imagine being interrupted and consider where to resume. Watching somebody else speak may provide useful examples, but it is different from privately imagining one’s own next action. Both can be followed by practice with real listeners.

The limits matter because imagination tends to supply conditions that are convenient. A cooperative listener in thought may ask a clear question; an actual visitor may ask something unexpected. Rehearsal should therefore leave a plan open to revision rather than freeze it into a script that must work. Isha’s experience illustrates a preparatory use of imagination: making assumptions noticeable enough to test. It does not make confidence a substitute for evidence about performance.

options.text: A. A rule requiring every uncertain gap to be filled immediately.
B. A controller using the damage map and permitted pattern rules.
C. The weight of a real surface resting on a frame.
D. An organism’s response to a severed limb.

questions.material:
D1

Researchers in a fictional project at Greyford Lab have constructed a digital model that restores a simple surface pattern after a unit is removed. The project is concerned with coordinating a sequence of decisions. It does not show that an organism regrows a limb or that a computer can recover the true history of an object when the evidence is missing.

The model combines a damage map with a set of permitted local patterns. First, a process marks the damaged position, distinguishing an empty place from a unit that is present but differently coloured. The controller then checks the neighbouring pattern against its stored rules and directs a matching unit into the gap. A final comparison verifies whether the joins are consistent. The rules guide placement; they are not a physical frame supporting a real surface.

In some trials, the surrounding units supported more than one possible completion. The model then flagged the gap as unresolved instead of announcing that one guess had recovered the original. This distinction was central to the design: producing a neat pattern and identifying a uniquely supported reconstruction are not the same thing. The reported success concerned gaps for which the permitted rules selected one completion.

The researchers hope to improve the repair of modular surfaces by learning how local information can guide coordinated replacement. Before any physical application, they would need to investigate materials, forces, wear and cases with incomplete information. A digital join that satisfies a rule says nothing by itself about whether a physical joint can carry a load.

The report is positive about the model’s ability to expose where a decision is supported and where it remains uncertain. Its promise lies partly in the refusal to hide unresolved cases. Further work is presented as testing those boundaries, rather than simply increasing the number of attractive completed patterns. The model offers a design principle to explore, not a finished method for repairing every damaged object.

questions.material:
A1

Baystone School certificate requirements

The following rules belong to an invented school. Students must meet all the requirements to receive its upper-school certificate.

Compulsory credits

4 credits in English (one credit in each of Years 9–12)

3 credits in mathematics (including at least one credit in Year 11 or 12)

2 credits in project courses from the three approved groups

2 credits in science

1 credit in community history

1 credit in local geography

1 credit in the arts

1 credit in health and physical education

1 credit in an additional language

0.5 credit in career studies

0.5 credit in civic participation

Optional credits

Students must earn 11 optional credits from approved courses. Up to 4 of these optional credits may come from approved partner-college courses; they are included, not added to the optional total.

Online learning

Students who entered Year 9 in September 2026 or later must complete at least 2 credits online. These online credits count within the compulsory or optional requirements above; they are not extra credits.

Literacy requirement

The literacy rule takes effect on 1 November 2026. Students graduating in 2026–2027 or later must satisfy the school’s literacy check as well as its credit requirements.

Community involvement

At least 40 hours of approved community activity are required. These hours are not course credits. Before beginning, students must:

check that the proposed activity meets the school’s approval rules;

consult the school’s list of approved and prohibited activities;

discuss the plan with a parent or guardian if they are under 18.

Students aged 18 or over must still verify that an activity qualifies, but the parent-or-guardian discussion rule does not apply to them.

options.text: A. The tilted box might move because its fastening was loose.
B. Maintenance had proved that all birds would return.
C. Every listed box had already been inspected and found empty.
D. The box had been removed from all reserve records.

questions.material:
B1

During an inspection in the fictional Merrow Bird Reserve, volunteer coordinator Sal noticed a nesting box tilted on its mounting post. A loose fastening could allow the box to move in strong wind. She recorded its number and referred it for inspection before it was put back into use. The team did not treat a box’s presence on the reserve’s list as proof that it remained in suitable condition.

Sal began by helping to organise the team’s observation notebooks. She learned that a brief entry such as “empty box” could leave important questions unanswered: had a volunteer looked inside at an authorised inspection, or merely seen no activity from the usual observation point? She now trains new members to record what kind of observation they actually made rather than turn an absence of sightings into a confident conclusion.

Maintenance workers reinforced the mounting assembly during a scheduled repair. They added supports to make it stronger, instead of replacing the whole box or only improving its appearance. Volunteers recorded the repair date and kept that information with later observations. A change after maintenance could then be considered in its proper context, rather than being treated as an unexplained event.

Two neighbourhood groups observe separate sections of the reserve. They now use the same box numbers and distinguish maintenance records from wildlife observations. When both groups described one box, the shared number revealed that their entries concerned the same object, not two different boxes. Their discussions also helped explain why a temporarily unavailable box should not be counted as an inspected empty one.

Sal welcomes the clearer records, but she does not claim that new supports alone determine whether birds use a box. Conditions and the timing of visits differ. Continued observation is still needed, and an uncertain entry is kept uncertain until there is a reason to revise it. Members need the persistence to return and the skill to separate what they saw, what was repaired and what they merely expected. Those distinctions make cooperation more useful than a larger total of unexplained notes.

options.text: A. By describing the author’s first concert abroad.
B. By giving results from a large leadership experiment.
C. By presenting an imagined preparation for leading music.
D. By listing official rules for laboratory safety.

questions.material:
C1

Picture a student preparing to lead a short piece of music. Before the group arrives, he mentally moves through the opening: waiting for quiet, giving a signal and listening for the first entry. In the fictional account that follows, this imagined sequence serves as preparation for a shared activity. It is not a substitute for hearing what the group actually does.

Student leader Owen first imagined an opening in which everybody responded immediately. When his tutor asked him to picture a delayed entry, he realised that he had no plan for restarting calmly. He considered a second signal and then tried it during a real rehearsal. Thinking through an alternative did not make the interruption happen; it made a response available to test if the interruption occurred.

Owen later said that he felt calmer about giving the first signal. That report does not establish a change in every player’s timing, a permanent improvement in his leadership or a measured effect on his nervous system. The account gives one person’s experience and one practical adjustment. It would be a mistake to treat all those different outcomes as though they had been assessed together.

The process can be applied to other sequences. A guide might privately picture greeting a visitor who asks an unexpected question. A laboratory presenter could imagine putting down one object before picking up another. These examples involve imagining one’s own actions and possible responses. Simply listing facts about a task is different, although factual preparation may be necessary before a useful sequence can be imagined.

A mental version of an event can also leave out the very difficulty that needs attention. Owen’s first imagined group was conveniently ready and cooperative. The tutor’s question helped him inspect that assumption. The value of this kind of rehearsal therefore lies partly in revising an imagined scene and then checking it against experience. It can support preparation without guaranteeing confidence, physical skill or the response of other people.

options.text: A. Mental rehearsal can support preparation when assumptions are questioned and tested.
B. An imagined cooperative group predicts exactly how real people will respond.
C. Feeling calm proves a permanent improvement in leadership.
D. Thinking through a task removes the need to prepare facts.

questions.material:
C1

Picture a student preparing to lead a short piece of music. Before the group arrives, he mentally moves through the opening: waiting for quiet, giving a signal and listening for the first entry. In the fictional account that follows, this imagined sequence serves as preparation for a shared activity. It is not a substitute for hearing what the group actually does.

Student leader Owen first imagined an opening in which everybody responded immediately. When his tutor asked him to picture a delayed entry, he realised that he had no plan for restarting calmly. He considered a second signal and then tried it during a real rehearsal. Thinking through an alternative did not make the interruption happen; it made a response available to test if the interruption occurred.

Owen later said that he felt calmer about giving the first signal. That report does not establish a change in every player’s timing, a permanent improvement in his leadership or a measured effect on his nervous system. The account gives one person’s experience and one practical adjustment. It would be a mistake to treat all those different outcomes as though they had been assessed together.

The process can be applied to other sequences. A guide might privately picture greeting a visitor who asks an unexpected question. A laboratory presenter could imagine putting down one object before picking up another. These examples involve imagining one’s own actions and possible responses. Simply listing facts about a task is different, although factual preparation may be necessary before a useful sequence can be imagined.

A mental version of an event can also leave out the very difficulty that needs attention. Owen’s first imagined group was conveniently ready and cooperative. The tutor’s question helped him inspect that assumption. The value of this kind of rehearsal therefore lies partly in revising an imagined scene and then checking it against experience. It can support preparation without guaranteeing confidence, physical skill or the response of other people.

options.text: A. A new link grown from living tissue.
B. A public bridge carrying normal traffic.
C. An instruction to activate every link without checking information.
D. A controller combining position codes with a stored layout.

questions.material:
D1

A fictional engineering team at Lenton Studio has tested a tabletop network that changes how it supports a light load when a connection weakens. The project is an investigation of sensing and coordination. It is not evidence that living tissue can be repaired, nor a demonstration that a design is safe for a public bridge.

The network contains prebuilt links, small sensors and a controller holding a layout of their positions. A sensor first identifies a weak connection. It passes a position code to the controller, which compares the code with the layout and activates a supporting link nearby. A second reading checks whether the load has been redistributed as intended. The system does not grow a new link; it selects from links already built into the model.

This sequence distinguishes detecting a weakness from responding appropriately to it. In a trial with an incomplete layout, a warning was produced but the controller could not reliably choose the nearby support. The researchers also tested signals that did not indicate an actual weak connection. Those trials mattered because a system that activates supports unnecessarily may create a different problem rather than simply provide extra protection.

The team’s long-term aim is to design monitoring systems for repairable structures. That goal would require evidence far beyond the tabletop demonstration: different loads, outdoor conditions, repeated changes and human inspection procedures would all have to be considered. The current model says nothing sufficient about a particular real building’s safety, and the report does not recommend installing it in one.

The authors are encouraged by the clear division of roles among sensing, information checking and response. They present the mechanism as a useful idea to investigate, with failures supplying information for later designs. Its promise is not that a warning automatically makes a structure safe. It is that a coordinated response can be studied step by step, including the circumstances in which the information needed for that response is missing.

options.text: A. Its reflected light from shore ice.
B. Its old marks above an arch.
C. Its distinctive nesting colony.
D. Its record length in the region.

questions.material:
The following fictional coastal and lakeside caves offer four different subjects for a visitor-centre exhibition. The descriptions concern their features and viewing programmes, not instructions for entering caves.

A1

Swift Chamber
A sheltered sea chamber on the north coast has become known for the island’s only recorded nesting colony of silver-wing swifts, an invented bird in this account. Cameras relay images from the nesting ledges to a viewing room above the bay. Although the entrance looks enormous from the water, the exhibition makes no claim that this is the region’s longest cave. Its reputation rests chiefly on the nesting colony rather than its size.

A2

Mirror Cove
This lakeside cave is presented through a different exhibition each season. The winter display is particularly popular: low sunlight reflects from a sheet of shore ice and sends moving patterns onto the entrance wall. Visitors watch the effect from the centre’s enclosed gallery. The programme does not involve walking across the frozen lake. Summer displays concentrate on the lake’s changing water level and are not advertised as the best time to see the reflected winter patterns.

A3

Blue Shaft
The roof of an old chamber has collapsed, leaving a deep, circular opening connected to the bay. In the fictional visitor programme, a boat with a viewing screen carries people above the opening while an underwater camera shows its lower walls. The attraction lies in seeing a vertical structure from the water rather than following a dry walking tunnel. The exhibition notes that its depth is not a measure of its age.

A4

Copper Arch
Bands of reddish stone give this cave its name. A boat-based tour stays outside the arch while a guide explains the stripes visible on the walls. No underwater camera is used here: the coloured layers can be seen directly from the boat. A narrow ledge above the arch contains old survey marks, but it is not part of the visitor route. The tour’s focus is the pattern of the rock rather than nesting birds.

options.text: A. Through shared work on a university magazine.
B. Through a reunion after their businesses closed.
C. Through an emergency-service training course.
D. Through their grandchildren’s archive project.

questions.material:
B1

When eight students first squeezed into a university print room in 1982, they were united by a practical problem: the campus magazine needed to reach readers, and the small press kept jamming. They spent evenings cleaning rollers, arguing over headlines and carrying finished pages across the wet courtyard. Somewhere between the deadlines, they became friends. Someone called them the Night Printers, and the name survived long after the magazine changed its equipment.

Now living in six different towns, the eight still arrange an annual weekend together. Their shared calendar contains birthdays, hospital visits and the dates when somebody needs help moving house. “I never have to build a rescue team from scratch,” says Leena, one of the group. “The team is already there.” She is not talking about an emergency service, but about friends who know when a short message means more than it says.

Staying close has required deliberate work. They alternate the location of reunions, check travel costs before making plans and leave space for those who cannot join a video call. None claims that a group chat can replace every meeting. Occasionally a missed message has caused hurt, and a long conversation has been needed to settle it. Yet they describe the effort as worthwhile because familiarity allows them to offer the kind of help that a newly made acquaintance might not know is needed.

When Arun closed his printing business, he was reluctant to tell anyone how unsettled he felt. A friend from the group invited him to repair old books on Saturday mornings. The invitation did not reopen his business or solve every financial problem. It did give him a regular reason to leave home and talk while his hands were busy. He later said that being useful alongside a friend mattered more than receiving another speech about staying positive.

The connection has spread beyond the original eight. Their children exchange books, and two of their grandchildren now help label photographs for the group archive. At a recent reunion, a daughter asked why the album contained so many pictures of an unreliable printing press. “That machine made us stay in the same room,” Leena replied. “We chose to keep returning after we no longer had to.”
